iOS 27 gave your iPhone an alarm feature that’s long been missing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.
  • Sources indicate that have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm?
  • It has been revealed that I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Sources indicate that have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

It has been revealed that I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a new volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

Do you plan to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

Hierarchical Bayesian Neural Networks: When Structure Meets Flexibility

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Statwonk

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we showed that Bayesian hierarchical models (BHMs) win when group structure is describable, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) win when the signal is complex, and their ensemble hedges across both scenarios.
  • It has been revealed that but what about the case where your data has both — known group structure and complex nonlinear signal?
  • In a recent development, enter the hierarchical Bayesian neural network (HBNN) — a model that combines partial pooling over groups with a flexible neural network function class.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we showed that Bayesian hierarchical models (BHMs) win when group structure is describable, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) win when the signal is complex, and their ensemble hedges across both scenarios.

It has been revealed that but what about the case where your data has both — known group structure and complex nonlinear signal? Neither the BHM nor the BNN is ideal:.

In a recent development, enter the hierarchical Bayesian neural network (HBNN) — a model that combines partial pooling over groups with a flexible neural network function class. This post adds the HBNN to our comparison and reveals when each of the four approaches excels.

The HBNN adds partially-pooled group intercepts to the neural network. The non-centered parameterization lets Stan explore the posterior efficiently:.

Sources indicate that line by line, this is a BNN with one addition: alpha[g[n]] — a group-specific intercept drawn from a learned population distribution. The neural network learns the shared nonlinear signal f(x), and the hierarchical intercepts capture group-level shifts. Each component does what it's best at.

The signal is linear and the heterogeneity is in group-specific intercepts and slopes. The BHM is perfectly specified — its functional form matches the DGP exactly. The HBNN's neural network component adds unnecessary flexibility here, making it a close second but slightly less efficient due to the additional parameters.

It has been revealed that no group-level heterogeneity — the group labels are noise. Both the BHM and the HBNN waste capacity estimating group intercepts that don't exist, but the BNN focuses entirely on learning the nonlinear signal. The HBNN is close because partial pooling drives the unnecessary group intercepts toward zero, but the BNN's simpler parameterization gives it an edge.

It has been revealed that now the data has both group-specific offsets and a complex nonlinear signal. This is the scenario the HBNN was built for:.

↓ Lower CRPS = lower out-of-sample prediction error (winner).

The HBNN isn't always the best model — it's the best model when the data has the structure it's designed for. That's the No Free Lunch theorem in action: every model has a niche, and the art is matching the model to the problem.

Recent findings suggest that in domains like portfolio optimization, clinical trials, and marketing mix modeling, the data often has exactly this structure: known grouping variables (sectors, treatment arms, channels) with complex nonlinear effects. The HBNN architecture — encoding the structure you know and learning the rest — represents a principled middle ground between pure specification and pure flexibility.

According to recent reports, the complete R script is available at hbnn_comparison_reprex.R. It requires cmdstanr, scoringRules, and tidyverse. Runtime is approximately 4–5 minutes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looking for something new to watch this weekend? Don't just sit around in a turkey haze when you can wake up your senses with the pulse-pounding thrillers newly available on Prime Video. Each week, I comb through the streaming service's latest additions to hunt down the suspenseful picks actually worth carving out time for.

November's new-arrivals shelf is still buried under holiday movies, so I dug through the tinsel to find three standout thrillers for your queue. I'll grant that one leans a little more action than pure suspense — an '80s hostage-rescue caper starring Chuck "Walker, Texas Ranger" Norris — but it packs more than enough tension to earn its spot alongside a razor-sharp Cold War mind-bender and a blood-soaked modern thriller about a rogue CIA assassin.

In a recent development, all three are well worth adding to your watchlist before the leftovers run out. Let's get into the three latest-to-Prime Video thrillers I'd recommend streaming this week. You'll be glad you didn't just eat and sleep over Thanksgiving weekend.

In a recent development, if you only stream one of my picks this week, make it this one. More than sixty years later, John Frankenheimer's "The Manchurian Candidate" is still one of the best political thrillers, and it feels surprisingly fresh. Frank Sinatra gives one of his finest screen performances as Major Bennett Marco, but it's Angela Lansbury who makes one of cinema's most monstrous mothers years ahead of her turn in "Murder, She Wrote.".

During the Korean War, a U.S. Army platoon is captured and brainwashed by Communists, and Sergeant Raymond Shaw (Laurence Harvey) comes home a decorated war hero. He has no memory that he's been reprogrammed as a sleeper assassin, triggered by the sight of a particular playing card. Marco (Sinatra), plagued by the same recurring nightmare as the other survivors, starts investigating, and the conspiracy leads straight to Shaw's domineering mother (Lansbury) and her senator husband (James Gregory) as the culprits.

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now.

I'm not going to sugarcoat it: "Delta Force" is prime cheese, the kind of action thriller where Chuck Norris mows down terrorists from a rocket-launching motorcycle. It's got an absurd bench of old-school talent, led by Lee Marvin in his final film role as the gravel-voiced Colonel Nick Alexander, and it'll keep you on the edge of your seat.

Loosely inspired by the 1985 hijacking of TWA Flight 847, the film follows an elite U.S. commando unit sent in after Lebanese militants seize a passenger jet and reroute it to Beirut. Norris plays Major Scott McCoy, who's pulled back into service to rescue the hostages. If you want to check out a gem with plenty of explosions and unexpected twists, this is one of the best in Norris's early catalogue.

Watch "Delta Force" on Prime Video now.

In a recent development, not to be confused with the Vince Vaughn–Owen Wilson comedy, this 2026 "Internship" is an R-rated action thriller with a nasty streak. It follows a CIA-trained killer, raised from childhood in a secret program that recruited kids under the cover of an "internship," who sets out to burn the agency down.

Lizzy Greene takes the lead role as Renee, the assassin who rallies her fellow "interns" into a bloody uprising against the organization that stole their childhoods, forcing the CIA to answer with equally lethal force. Megan Boone ("The Blacklist") and Sullivan Stapleton ("Blindspot") round out the ensemble.

Watch "The Internship on Prime Video now.

Industry News: Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Quad9

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French customers.
  • In a recent development, we are unhappy to have reached this impasse.
  • Recent findings suggest that we have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so owners in France cannot resolve those DNS names.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French customers. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond rapidly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours.

In a recent development, we are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see our announcement of this deactivation from one month ago.

Recent findings suggest that we have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so owners in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Currently, the courts have upheld beInâs demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties.

We have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and counter-productive effort, but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines.

This is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: owners who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9.

We object to the core premise of the legal arguments, which is the false assertion that recursive DNS can or should be used as a method to prevent piracy or any other type of content access. Our position is this is not effective or useful, as we have no monopoly on recursive DNS, and anyone can set up their own resolver in just a few seconds (though without the privacy and malicious content protection that Quad9 offers). The courts and plaintiff have not considered this argument and ignore it entirely in the judgement. Their interest is focused on the possibility for us to do what is demanded, even if it has results outside of France, and their interest is not in why that is unjust or unwise or ineffective. So, we will continue to argue with a refutation of our ability to do this accurately without applying French law to all other European nations and the world.

It has been revealed that there is an understandable focus on how Quad9 is going to block “French people” when we do not collect user information and have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names. We understand this seemingly apparent paradox, so we will expand on it as it is a question that is frequently repeated.

In a recent development, our geoIP-based method to identify and deny service to French users is inexact. We are aware that our methods to geographically locate users and declare they are in France is quite imprecise - this is inevitable. By using these methods, we will create conditions of overblocking, where we accidentally classify some queries as being from France when they are not from France, and it will also result in conditions of underblocking, where we do not correctly identify some queries as being from France and inappropriately complete those requests even though the user is in French jurisdiction. This imprecision is a core component of our case: there is no legally accurate way for us to determine what queries are from users located in France versus what queries are from users not in France. But we have no other mechanism - it simply does not exist.Â.

Industry observers note that these geoIP lists are inaccurate in two dimensions: firstly, IP geolocation data are often imprecise or just plain wrong, as IP geolocation is not an exact science. Mobile operators span national boundaries, corporate WANs split networks across nations, IP addresses are bought and sold frequently, and network operators shift allocations across borders. These are just a few of many other examples of how geoIP association may not be accurate. Secondly, IP location does not necessarily equate to user location, geoIP data only is a guess as to the location of the IP address, not the location of the end user. VPNs may exit in France but have the majority of their owners in other nations; corporate users in one nation may egress in another due to proxies or internal DNS service distribution - there is nothing about a query that has any indication of the jurisdiction of the origin of the query itself.

According to recent reports, the data is imprecise, but we do not know to what level it is imprecise. So we must work with what we have.

Sources indicate that we could apply this same geoIP filter database to selectively block French users from reaching the sites we have been told to make unavailable, but this would corrupt our core premise which is that the DNS is not the right mechanism for this blocking to happen. If we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users - we lose our integrity and still do not have legally perfect coverage, plus we will inevitably apply French rulings across borders into other nations. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission which is to only block cyber risks to end users and not content. Secondarily, we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us.Â.

Recent findings suggest that by accepting even the smallest of the demands for blocking based on geoIP data, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we accept to play a complicit role in aiding companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint. We would be admitting that DNS blocking is a valid instrument for the piracy problem - it is not. We would be admitting we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not. We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of content filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not.

So we accept there will be egregious overblocking/underblocking errors in our blockade of French owners but would rather remain steadfast to our stated mission and principles to uphold the integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you receive the DNS as you (the user) expect, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.

In a recent development, quad9 blocks a set of cyber-threats on 9.9.9.9 (and secondary IPs) for end customers, where the outcome would be an unexpected and harmful result to the end user (i.e., malicious software). Content blocking is explicitly not in that set. Quad9 has subjective editing on that set, as well - if we believe something is inappropriately categorized by our threat intelligence partners, then we can remove it at our discretion. Additionally, Quad9 also offers 9.9.9.10, which has no blocking of any kind - it is entirely open. The demands we have been given would enforce mandatory restrictions on all our service addresses, which then makes our statements of their functionality inconsistent with the reality that would be forced upon us. We will not accept that condition.

We take a long range and principled view to the outcome of this case and the others in line. There are unmistakable long-term risks to Quad9, to user privacy, and to potential fragmentation of the internet that are far beyond the current moment. To give in now would start âthe beginning of the endâ and allow motion towards internet fragmentation that cannot be undone. We accept the risks and the pain that come with fighting where others in similar circumstances to ourselves must bend and compromise in this invisible card game where end users are not even at the table. We represent those users, and our nonprofit mission of public service is aptly unique by not representing any shareholders, products, or other interests other than the end user.Â.

It is especially disturbing to us to be doing this for an issue (piracy) which we believe is not slowed at all by any involvement of recursive DNS, though the damage to the integrity and trust of the global namespace is significant.

Industry observers note that we have seen recent articles about extended blocking demands given to ISPs in France of social media or instant messaging sites, which we anticipate would be demanded of us as well if continued. It is quite clear to us the path that is being taken with these efforts: first create the mechanism, then expand the volumes of the mechanism (unconstrained rightsholder editing of the DNS), then expand the scope of prohibitions to other groups and for other reasons until there is effectively no limit to the number of editors or the reasons for DNS names to be deleted from recursive resolution. This contradicts our mission of delivery of trustworthy DNS results, and we believe this potential outcome to be antithetical to a free and open internet.

This is the second legal assault we have faced to see if the DNS can be slowly corrupted - we stood our ground and eventually won in Germany; with the continued community sponsorship and support we hope to win here, too. We refuse to take even the smallest step towards building the machinery of mandatory DNS restriction, and we will not abandon our obligation to the security, privacy, and integrity we have mentioned we will deliver to users worldwide. We deeply regret having to step back from France and hope we will be able to return some day and offer the same unfiltered services that the rest of the world enjoys.Â.

Legal battles like this drain time and resources away from building a better, safer internet. Your financial support is what keeps us in the fightâand keeps our services free and open for everyone. If you stand with us, please consider donating or becoming a sponsor today.

MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

Industry observers note that the MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

Industry observers note that the single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker states that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Recent findings suggest that anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

Sources indicate that there’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

#109070. 10 Hidden Controls Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

10 Hidden Controls Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can have a ton of fun in GTA 6 even if you only follow the core gameplay loop of running around, stealing cars, and completing missions and side quests.
  • According to recent reports, if you just want to sit back and relax as your character drives around Leonida in GTA 6, you should try the auto-drive mode.
  • Your character is going to commit a lot of crimes in GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can have a ton of fun in GTA 6 even if you only follow the core gameplay loop of running around, stealing cars, and completing missions and side quests. However, if you take a minute to learn a few hidden controls, I think you'll enjoy the game even more. These are fairly simple controls that let you hide from the cops, trash talk other drivers, or flip the bird when you're feeling like annoying NPCs. These are 10 of the best hidden GTA 6 controls that'll help you unlock an entirely latest side of the game.

According to recent reports, if you just want to sit back and relax as your character drives around Leonida in GTA 6, you should try the auto-drive mode. It's a relaxing way to enjoy the streets without having to worry about following traffic rules. To enable it, you need to get in a vehicle and add a waypoint on the map. This serves as your character's destination, so if you want a longer drive, be sure to drop the waypoint far, far away. Next, hold the down arrow on the D-Pad, and press the Option button. This enables cinematic mode. Then, hold the Circle button to enable auto-drive.

Your character is going to commit a lot of crimes in GTA 6. When this happens, you attract heat, and soon enough, cops will begin chasing you. Switching cars is a great way to reduce the amount of attention you get from law enforcement, but you can still be identified by your face or clothing. Until you can reach a safe spot to swap outfits, maintain a low profile by ducking while driving. Hold the Circle button while driving to duck.

Sources indicate that EA's Road Rash was among the first racing games I played as a child, and I remember how much fun it was to kick your rivals while speeding through the game's various courses. You can have a taste of that in GTA 6 too. Press the Square button while you're riding a bike, and your character will kick anyone who's near you. If you do this in a car, it opens the door, and hits people around the car. To annoy other drivers, press R3, and your character will direct some trash talk towards NPCs.

Industry observers note that hold Circle to lean back against walls, or to sit on the beach. To rest on a ledge, you can hold L3. This lets you take a moment to soak in beautiful views in the game, or lounge around as you listen to NPC conversations. Paying attention to those conversations can lead to some fun side quests, and sometimes give you a tip or two for quick money or other rewards.

In a recent development, if you really want to rile people up in GTA 6, you can flip the bird. This works only when your character is unarmed. Hold L2, focus on a person, then press R1. Actions have consequences in GTA 6, so be prepared to fight NPCs when you do this.

When you're being chased by cops, enemies, or angry NPCs, you can use a quick shortcut to look back without turning the camera around. Just hold R3 to look behind you.

While driving, press Circle to toggle headlights (and switch to high beams). This is particularly useful when you're offroading at night. You can also hold left arrow on the D-Pad, and move the right stick up to access other vehicle controls like hazard lights, opening or closing windows, etc., in case you want to add to the realism.

According to recent reports, stealing emergency vehicles in GTA 6 is risky, but the reward is totally worth it. Not only do you find stashes of weapons, gear, and money in some of these vehicles, but you also have access to sirens that help you clear traffic off your path. If you steal an ambulance or a cop car, hold L3, and move the left stick up to go through different siren tones. Press L3 and the left stick up to enable the siren.

GTA 6 is a third-person game, but it has a first-person mode that partially works. It is useful for looking at smaller objects around your character, such as posters, small signs, or to look for clues in and around a house. (Yes, I am talking about Mandy's creepy house and bad vibes.) Hold L2 + hit R3 to switch to first-person mode. Sadly, you can't move when you do this, but you can look around. Try it in Mandy's property to observe a few nasty surprises.

Industry observers note that when you sprint towards a car, press the X button to slide across the hood. This is much faster and smoother than running around parked cars or jumping over them. It also looks cool, which is reason enough to try this feature.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that wu-Tang Clan has substantial prepares for Thanksgiving.
  • Wu-Tang, founded in Staten Island, NY, has long been considered one of the most influential groups in music history, with legions of fans worldwide and even their own acolytes known as the Killa Bees, a collective of rappers, producers, singers and others affiliated with the group.
  • The remarkable story of how Cilvaringz became associated with Wu-Tang and then played a critical role in producing the astonishing one-copy only album Once Upon a Time in Shaolin is told in the documentary The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable, now streaming on Netflix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that wu-Tang Clan has substantial prepares for Thanksgiving. The hip-hop legends will be in Detroit to headline the halftime show for the NFL game between the host Lions and the Chicago Bears (U2 will do the halftime honors for the Thanksgiving Eve game in LA between the Green Bay Packers and the Los Angeles Rams, airing on Netflix).

Wu-Tang, founded in Staten Island, NY, has long been considered one of the most influential groups in music history, with legions of fans worldwide and even their own acolytes known as the Killa Bees, a collective of rappers, producers, singers and others affiliated with the group. Among the most notable Bees: Cilvaringz, aka Tarik Azzougarh, a Dutch Moroccan Wu-Tang superfan turned artist whose connection to the Clan goes back to the late 1990s.

The remarkable story of how Cilvaringz became associated with Wu-Tang and then played a critical role in producing the astonishing one-copy only album Once Upon a Time in Shaolin is told in the documentary The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable, now streaming on Netflix. Watch on Deadline.

The Oscar-contending film is directed by Joanna Natasegara, the Academy Award-winning producer of The White Helmets, The Edge of Democracy, Virunga and other acclaimed documentaries. The Disciple premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January and screened in September at the Telluride Film Festival before debuting on Netflix.

In a recent development, DEADLINE: Have you always been into Wu-Tang? When did you learn about the story of Tarik Azzougarh?

Joanna Natasegara: I grew up in the ’90s. It’s exactly my era of music… Wu-Tang was just something me and my friends were very much into. We would go to clubs and listen to hip hop music, but it was something I just didn’t really think about in the scope of my work, clearly for decades, actually. And so, the story [of Tarik/Cilvaringz] itself I hadn’t heard of despite it being something that had gone around the world.

I was on a holiday in Morocco with my family and a script writer friend of mine came for lunch and she remarked, “My brother [Tarik] is having some trouble with his life story and his life rights.” And I was like, “Okay.” I knew he was Moroccan, but I thought [his story] would be something that pertained to North Africa, not to Staten Island. And she said, “Do you know the Wu-Tang?” I was like, “Yeah. I don’t really know where this is going.” [She said], “He’s a Killer Bee.” And I was like, “How is that possible?” And so, she told me a little part of the story, but she said, “It’s so convoluted, complicated, twisty, wonderful. Can I bring him to lunch tomorrow?”.

So, he came to lunch and honestly, over a three-hour lunch, he told me his whole life story. And not only did I think it was a great story, it just really resonated. We’re exactly the same age. He was obviously a migrant growing up in a tiny town in Europe, and a lot of that resonated with me and he was very ambitious to make it [in the music business], and I thought that was really inspiring.

In a recent development, DEADLINE: It’s a very complex story to tell as your feature directorial debut. About halfway into The Disciple, you really start to pivot to the sale of the kind of one-off album, Once Upon a Time in Shaolin. But as an audience we really need to understand how it all came together. We need to understand Cilvaringz, Tarik, and that’s complicated. So, this is not an easy piece of storytelling to do.

JN: No, no, no, it wasn’t… I wanted to build the film as a kind of homage to a Wu-Tang album. There’s a lot of Easter eggs in the film — if you’re a Clan fan, you can see them. But I also wanted the film to work for somebody that didn’t know anything about the Wu-Tang. So that’s a tricky balance to be able to tell a story that’s not too complex, but also dense enough for the mega fans, and there are millions of them.

In a recent development, I was well held by two extremely experienced editors, Chloe Lambourne who cut for For Sama and Chris Dickens who cut for Slumdog Millionaire. And that was a lot of fun.

DEADLINE: The film does work for people who are not steeped in either hip hop or Wu-Tang or martial arts movies or “pharma bro” Martin Shkreli [who bought the one-copy only album] or other elements of the story.

According to recent reports, JN: It’s a coming-of-age story and a story about ambition because I think that’s what Tarik took from RZA, what RZA took from Shifu [Shaolin monk Shi Yan Ming] and what audiences are seeming to take from Tarik. So, the album in a way is kind of a McGuffin. Obviously, some people are very attracted to know about the machinations of the album, but I’m really interested in the mentorship aspect of the film.

Recent findings suggest that DEADLINE: There’s the line that RZA says: “Persistence overcomes resistance,” and it’s wonderful. That motto guided Tarik as a protégé of RZA and Wu-Tang, but it could also apply to you as a filmmaker.

According to recent reports, JN: It’s great, isn’t it? We had t-shirts made.

In a recent development, DEADLINE: Towards the end of the film, you ask Tarik specifically whether producing Once Upon a Time in Shaolin was a career highlight or if it destroyed his career. And his answer is quite interesting, that he doesn’t necessarily think of himself as having a career.

JN: I think he’s quite honest and reflective in the piece. I thank him for that trust because that’s notable, isn’t it, in documentary? And I think he is reflective about that process, but he’s also resilient and knew what that meant to do that [album]. I think they both did, him and RZA, but the discussion [it ignited] was the point [about the value attached to a work of music] and that has worked. People are seeing that stunt and the value of music because of it. And I think it’s inspired many other people to do similar things.

According to recent reports, the album was a perfect protest. It was a perfect way to say, why is this piece of music worth less than something that is put in an extraordinary museum? So, I think it was a really clever protest piece, and to that extent it’s also worked. We’re talking about it years later. So, it’s a conversation that’s endured and I think is really relevant not only to music now, but also to film or any piece of creative, especially as we move more and more into the dangers of AI. How much less will everything be valued, in fact?

It has been revealed that note: After Martin Shkreli’s conviction for fraud, the U.S. government seized his assets, including the one copy of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin encased in its custom-made box. Per a legal agreement, the album will not be available for commercial release until the year 2103. In the interim, it can only be played at limited special events.

DEADLINE: Probably the first question you get asked is, have you listened to the album?

In a recent development, JN: We had a beautiful listening session at Sundance, and then we had another one at Telluride. I haven’t heard the whole thing. And it’s probably the most frustrating thing about this film… I can’t show you how good the album is; that’s going to be a question for people, but it really is good… I still think all of us involved in the film or the album go back and debate, do we hope it’s released? Do we not? Is it better than it isn’t released? But I would really like people to be able to hear it because it’s good.

Industry News: AI May Be Scanning Your Private Signal Chats

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (419 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads.
  • Industry observers note that in a recent blog post, Signal president Meredith Whitaker outlined the potential threat AI assistants like Siri and Gemini pose to the platform's promise of privacy.
  • Signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you use Signal, it's likely you care at least a little bit about keeping your communication private so only you and those you're chatting with can see your message threads. Signal's end-to-end encryption keeps prying eyes out, but if you use agentic AI on your device, your chats may not be as locked down as you think.

Industry observers note that in a recent blog post, Signal president Meredith Whitaker outlined the potential threat AI assistants like Siri and Gemini pose to the platform's promise of privacy. Systems-level capabilities like Gemini Intelligence (on Android) and Siri AI's Onscreen Awareness (on iOS and macOS) scan your screen and may be able to capture data from Signal conversations in the process, which can then be used to perform tasks. Not only does this potentially expose your information, but that of other conversation participants as well. Whitaker notes that this leaves privacy protections outside of Signal's control because the platform cannot easily restrict AI access to the app.

Signal has already blocked screenshot capabilities for Microsoft's Recall AI, which by default was able to take and store screen grabs of Signal messages on Windows 11. While Signal cannot guarantee that AI won't have access to your data, there are a few protections now available for those on iOS and Android as well.

The main workaround in Signal for now is to restrict screenshots and screen recordings inside the app, though this does not prevent AI agents from potentially grabbing content from other parts of your device. According to Signal's support documents, these protections will now be enabled by default on iOS 27 and Android with the latest versions of the Signal app.

According to recent reports, customers on iOS 27 can confirm or manually disable screenshot protection via Settings > Privacy > Block Siri AI. The compromise with this setting is that it also blocks you from taking screenshots of Signal conversations in the app and App Switcher, though you can disable it temporarily for 10 minutes if needed. On Android, Signal automatically engages the "Screen security" setting when it detects an AI agent attempting to access the screen. This, too, blocks screenshots inside the app and can be disabled via Settings > Privacy > App security > Screen security. Signal cannot block screenshots on macOS 27. However, users can add Signal to their Excluded Apps list via System Settings > Siri, which at least limits proactive access to conversations by Siri AI.

Sources indicate that if you or someone on your shopping list wants a newly introduced smartwatch, you have plenty of options to choose from. The problem is, a lot of them can be quite pricey. Apple's cheapest smartwatch, the SE 3, starts at $249, and its other selections only skyrocket from there. On the flip side, the risk in picking a smartwatch that's too inexpensive is that the manufacturer likely made a series of sacrifices to get the price that low. At a certain point, the tradeoff just isn't worth it.

It has been revealed that luckily, you do have options. There are two smartwatches on the market that aren't just cheaper than the competition, they're not even in the same ballpark. And while you shouldn't expect the same capabilities as you would on flagship wearables, these devices are perfectly usable, both as fitness trackers and smartwatches—all while spending well below $100 a pop. CNET put both smartwatches through their paces to make these determinations, so you know whichever model you get, you won't be picking up a wearable paperweight.

Contrary to what you might expect, Amazfit has no ties to Amazon—other than that you can buy these watches from the latter. Amazfit is its own manufacturer, and produces a wide selection of smartwatch options. The Bip 6 happens to be the company's latest budget smartwatch, with an MSRP of just $79.99. In most cases, a price that low would be a red flag for a smartwatch, but not in the Bip 6's case.

Industry observers note that the Amazfit Bip 6 holds its own against other flagship smartwatches. That's true on a surface level: This watch looks your average smartwatch, rather than a cheap imitation. In fact, at first glance, I'd bet most people would assume the Bip 6 is actually an Apple Watch. It has a rounded square design with a large 1.97-inch display with a resolution of 390 by 450 pixels (though there's no Always-On display). This isn't a cheap display, either: Amazfit put an AMOLED screen on the watch, which looks great indoors—though CNET Labs struggled to see the screen in direct sunlight.

Where the Bip 6 really shines, however, is with fitness tracking. This watch supports GPS, which makes tracking outdoor runs possible without a smartphone. CNET Labs found that it takes about 10 seconds to find a GPS signal, but once it connects, you're set. While running, the Bip 6 reliably tracks your heart rate. CNET Labs compared its sensor to the Polar chest strap HR monitor and found it on par, though, like other smartwatches, the Bip 6 is slower at detecting heart rate spikes. You'll get data like cadence and stride while tracking runs, and strength training and muscle groups while working out indoors. For example, CNET Labs found that it correctly identified arm muscle exercises while testing the watch during a pilates session.

You also get some health and wellness features, too. The Bip 6 can measure heart rate variations, body temperature changes, sleep stages, and even your breathing quality. Its One Tap Measuring mode supports a single reading for heart rate, SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation), stress, and breathing rate, and it supports cycle tracking—though CNET specifies it can't track skin temperature like other smartwatches and health trackers. There's an optional subscription that provides AI coaching tools and looks out for health conditions like sleep apnea and insomnia. While health and wellness tracking is solid, note that CNET Labs found Amazfit's app, Zepp, to be confusing, since it simply displays your data without much context or explanation.

For an $80 smartwatch, the Bip 6 has an excellent battery life. CNET Labs found that the watch could be pushed to its limits—multiple workouts using GPS, heart rate tracking, keeping the display on during workouts—and still run for eight days before needing a charge. In fact, reviewer Vanessa Hand Orellana speculates you could push the Bip 6 to Amazfit's two-week battery life claim by limiting some of the most intensive settings and features. The only downside here is that there is no fast charging, so it will take about two hours to get back to 100%. But if you're only charging the watch once every week or two, that isn't much of a burden. There's also no charger in the box, so you'll need to use a separate USB-C cable.

Recent findings suggest that as a smartwatch, the Bip 6 can be a mixed bag. CNET found that the UI was clunky and sluggish, and the OS requires some user intervention before it's as usable as a standard Apple Watch or Galaxy Watch. While the watch has a voice assistant, Flow, CNET found it to be borderline unusable. However, CNET says Android people can reply to texts with a keyboard or dictation without needing the assistant. iPhone users can't do the same by default, but by downloading a third-party app, they can jerry-rig the watch to send and receive texts.

In a recent development, based on CNET Labs' testing, the Amazfit Bip 6 is one of the best budget smartwatches you can buy. For $80, you get a reliable workout tracker that looks like most standard watches on the market. And while you're making some sacrifices at this price point, they're largely worth it for $80.

Sources indicate that while the Amazfit is a good choice for both iPhone and Android consumers, the Galaxy Fit 3 might be the best choice for Samsung users. This isn't an option for iPhone users, and while it works with all Android devices, you get some Samsung-specific perks if you have a Galaxy phone.

The Galaxy Fit 3 is even cheaper than the Amazfit Bip 6: This watch is only $60, which makes it among the cheapest smartwatches you can buy. Now, this doesn't look like your average smartwatch. Samsung opted for a fitness tracker-like design, with a long 1.6-inch (40mm) AMOLED display. But for a fitness tracker/smartwatch hybrid, it's a solid look.

In CNET's testing, one of the Galaxy Fit 3's biggest strengths is its battery life—though it pales in comparison to the Bip 6. When pushed to its limits, the Fit 3 can run three days in between charges, though Samsung claims you can get it up to 13 days with the right settings. While the Amazfit has it beat, the Fit 3 might sound like a dream compared to other smartwatches, even from Samsung. Unlike the Bip 6, the Fit 3 supports fast charging. You can fill the watch up completely in just over an hour.

It has been revealed that CNET did find that the "smart" elements of this wearable were a bit lacking, however. The Fit 3 doesn't support voice dictation or mobile payments like other watches do, and unless you have a Galaxy phone, you won't be able to access the camera remote or sync your alarms. And while the Amazfit Bip 6's "Flow" is hardly reliable, the Fit 3 doesn't have an assistant at all. You can see incoming calls and decline (but not answer) them, and you can send prewritten responses to text messages, but not initiate them. Still, CNET found that Samsung added the essentials: You have an alarm, calculator, weather app, camera remote, and, of course, the Samsung Health app. (What kind of health tracker would this be without it?).

In a recent development, CNET found that the Fit 3 is a reliable fitness tracker, particularly for $60. You can track over 100 different workouts, and the watch automatically logs exercises like runs, walks, rowing, and elliptical sessions—if you enable auto-tracking, that is. It also supports swimming with its IP68 water resistance rating. CNET Labs found that the heart rate tracking was "generally accurate" when compared to the Polar chest strap, though its slower with registering heart rate spikes. Interestingly, the heart rate tracker was a bit delayed in testing, but once CNET reviewed the data in the health app, the data had corrected to be largely accurate. You also get high and low heart rate alerts, though no ECG app. (The $249 Apple Watch SE 3 also omits this feature.).

In CNET's testing, the sleep tracker on the Fit 3 was useful, if not entirely accurate. The watch can detect your sleep stages and look out for snoring using your Galaxy phone's mic. Like other health trackers, you get a sleep score, but CNET found it a bit inaccurate, since it rated a six and a half hour sleep session "Excellent" (91/100).

Recent findings suggest that still, the Fit 3 is really the only other smartwatch option at this price point that people should seriously consider. Until another firm drops a product around this MSRP, you have two solid choices in the Amazfit Bip 6 and Galaxy Fit 3.

The SlideTag’s extra features are controlled by the Kodak Memory Link app, while tracking is handled in the Find My app on iPhone just like an AirTag (and the Find Hub app on Android phones).

There are nine total styles for the SlideTag, all sold in a blind box format. You can order one tracker for $35 with the whole set also available for purchase.

Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar reveals how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

It has been revealed that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar demonstrates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session demonstrates how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also highlights how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

#109053. Three Reasons Not to Use ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ During Black Friday

Three Reasons Not to Use ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ During Black Friday

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales.
  • Sources indicate that while BNPL prepares can allow you to pay for purchases in installments without interest, they come with a cost that can easily outweigh any significant discounts.
  • According to recent reports, to be clear, Amazon doesn't have its own buy now, pay later program, and the firm is not uniquely misleading on this front.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gone are the days of needing to wait until after Thanksgiving to shop some seriously substantial Black Friday sales. As you're adding item after item to your cart during the sale, you might be tempted by offers for an "affordable monthly payment system." Also known as "buy now, pay later" (BNPL), the pitch is a tempting one: Buy what you need now, and pay later, "on your own timeline." But as convenient as it sounds, you should think twice before using buy now, pay later options, whether during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or at any other time.

Sources indicate that while BNPL prepares can allow you to pay for purchases in installments without interest, they come with a cost that can easily outweigh any significant discounts. Let's take a look at the hidden costs of BNPL, and why you're better off paying upfront for all your Black Friday purchases.

According to recent reports, to be clear, Amazon doesn't have its own buy now, pay later program, and the firm is not uniquely misleading on this front. The process is straightforward: you choose your items, select Affirm (a third-party lender) at checkout, complete a quick application, and receive an instant decision on your loan terms. Individual transactions initiated through Affirm are limited to $25,000, with a daily maximum of $100,000 across multiple purchases—but of course, your Black Friday splurge will be nowhere near that significant, right? (Right?!).

It has been revealed that the main draw of these programs is the ability to "pay at your own pace." If you are required to pay a down payment, that is due at the time of the transaction. From there, your first monthly payment is usually due one month after your purchase is processed. Each following payment will be due one month later, on the same day of the month.

You can choose your own timeline, usually spanning 3, 6, 12, or 24 months, depending on the purchase amount and your creditworthiness. Unlike traditional credit cards, Affirm shows you the exact payment amount and total cost upfront, and claims no hidden fees or compound interest.

You need a separate Affirm account in addition to your Amazon Prime membership. The application process requires basic information, including your name, mobile phone number, date of birth, and the last four digits of your Social Security number. Affirm performs a soft credit check initially, which doesn't impact your credit score, though they may conduct a hard inquiry for some loans.

BNPL aims are helpful if you really need to finance something major, but whenever possible, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses.

Industry observers note that the ease of this sort of financing can make expensive purchases feel more affordable than they actually are. When you can buy a $1,000 tablet for "just $67 per month," it's easy to lose sight of the total cost, as well as your overall financial picture. In turn, this makes it all too easy to overspend on items you might not have purchased otherwise. You're better off taking a breath, stepping away from your shopping cart, and setting alerts to be notified when a product hits a price you can stomach, at a time you can afford it.

Industry observers note that despite what you may have heard in the past, BNPL providers may report to credit bureaus, meaning your BNPL purchases can in fact affect your credit score. For instance, all Affirm payments (including on-time, late, and missed payments) are now reported to the credit bureau Experian. So if you miss payments or default on the installment initiative, it will cause damage to your credit score—making it even harder to get approved for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and other financing down the road.

Still, not all BNPL providers report to credit bureaus or use the same type of credit check, so it’s notable to understand the specific terms and practices of any service you’re considering.

Sources indicate that when you use a credit card, you get valuable purchase protections like extended warranty coverage, price protection, and the ability to dispute fraudulent charges. BNPL intends generally don't come with these safeguards. This means you're on the hook if something goes wrong with your BNPL purchase and the retailer doesn't make things right. The smarter move is to only buy what you can afford during a sale, no matter how tempting those deals may seem.

Recent findings suggest that although installment plans are helpful if you really need to finance something major, it’s best to avoid taking on debt for everyday expenses. Better to wait for a good price for something you truly need and can afford to pay for right now.

If there's a big-ticket item on sale for Black Friday but it's still out of your budget, consider these two questions before you turn to BNPL through Affirm:.

Industry observers note that is this really an essential purchase? BNPL should really only be used on completely necessary purchases that you can’t afford right now, but can afford in six weeks. On that note...

According to recent reports, will I be able to pay this off within six weeks? When a bigger payment gets broken down into smaller installments, you might find yourself overspending in the long run, because it "feels" like you can afford it. Stay on top of how much you’re actually spending—especially if you're considering multiple BNPL purchases—and how it will impact your overall budget going forward.

For more information about deals and discounts, keep an eye on all of Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage.

Sources indicate that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Industry observers note that the best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick, the man behind Grand Theft Auto VI, will speak at SXSW London 2027, organizers announced Tuesday.

Zelnick, who will talk “about building one of the world’s biggest entertainment franchises,” is among the first-wave of speakers for SXSW London, which returns to Shoreditch, east London, for its third year in May.

According to recent reports, built around the theme “The Power of Human Potential”, the 2027 festival will focus on people in a year dominated by what machines can do. Additional speakers include Jon Steinback, former DeepMind creative lead whose start-up Marker is building an AI writing tool designed to develop, rather than delete, writers. David Thornton, President of Genomics Limited, will explore how rapid analysis of large-scale genetic and genomic information will empower us to predict disease risks and improve medicine.

Rounding out the first group of speakers are Sir Martin Sorrell and Rory Sutherland and media personality GK Barry, who will discuss the future of advertising and the creator economy. Additionally, Refik Anadol, founder of the newly opened L.A. museum, Dataland, will share his artistic vision for AI and data-driven installations. Watch on Deadline.

The 2027 festival will run from May 24-29.

Sources indicate that in the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app released on the platform.

Now, that icon might be coming back.

Sources indicate that android Authority spotted several new app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta upgrade (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow owners to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

That remarked, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.
