  • Recent findings suggest that just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not.
  • Industry observers note that at its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cupertino is one of those TV reveals that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Recent findings suggest that just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

Industry observers note that at its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

Industry observers note that it’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a substantial-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, if you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

The true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the tech giant lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Early warning signs could help doctors predict those at risk of a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before an event, research suggests.
  • Scientists identified early patterns in a range of risk factors for cardiovascular disease – conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels – including high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney function.
  • They also revealed differences in the blood of those who went on to have a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke, more than a decade beforehand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early warning signs could help doctors predict those at risk of a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before an event, research suggests.

Scientists identified early patterns in a range of risk factors for cardiovascular disease – conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels – including high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney function.

They also revealed differences in the blood of those who went on to have a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke, more than a decade beforehand.

The findings highlight a large window of opportunity to intervene to reduce cardiovascular risk and prevent the development of serious disease, experts say.

Cardiovascular disease kills one in four people in the UK. Traditional risk factors, such as high blood pressure and cholesterol, have been widely linked to the risk of disease. However, previous studies have typically focused on a single risk factor and don’t monitor long-term changes.

Other influences, such as kidney function and biomarkers in the blood, could also play an important role in establishing disease risk.

A research team, led by the University of Edinburgh, examined data from more than 100,000 people between 1985 and 2019 to explore the patterns of multiple risk factors in relation to cardiovascular events over time.

The research, funded by the British Heart Foundation, included data from four population studies across the United States, Norway and the United Kingdom.

Systolic blood pressure – the pressure in arteries when the heart beats or contracts – was consistently higher in those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who were event-free, starting at 4 mmHg higher three decades before and increasing to 7 mmHg closer to the event.

Recent findings suggest that patterns were different between sexes throughout life. Younger women had lower blood pressure than younger men, but this switched around the age of 65, when female readings tended to be higher than males.

Researchers also identified important differences by age. Those who experienced a cardiovascular event at a younger age were more likely to have diabetes and a higher body mass index in the decades before the event.

Sources indicate that patterns in blood biomarkers also revealed early differences between those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who didn’t. Changes in the levels of a protein called NT-proBNP – used to monitor heart failure – could be seen up to 10 years beforehand.

Trajectories of other non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including physical activity and kidney function, also differed between individuals with and without cardiovascular events.

Tracking the course of risk factors over time may help to better predict serious cardiovascular events, experts say. Further research should also explore whether incorporating non-traditional risk factors could help to improve the estimation of cardiovascular disease risk, they add.

The study did not look at risk factors by ethnicity, and the team cautions that further research exploring potential differences in risk factor and biomarker trajectories across ethnic groups is needed.

I am excited about the findings of our study as they show that modifiable risk factors begin to diverge 30 years before a cardiovascular event occurs. This highlights a great opportunity to develop early prevention strategies throughout the life course, utilising the patterns of established and emerging risk factors and biomarkers to reduce future cardiovascular events.

For the vast majority of people, heart attacks and strokes are completely preventable. But many of us don’t realise we are at risk until it’s too late.

Recent findings suggest that this study adds to growing evidence that red flags for cardiovascular disease appear decades before it arrives. That could lead to a simple blood pressure reading, or proteins in the blood, being used to forewarn people of their future cardiovascular risk. Knowledge like this could empower people to make lifestyle changes or start treatment while they are still relatively young, which might reduce their risk, prevent a heart attack or stroke, and rewrite their future.

For now, it is worth remembering that we can all find out our risk of cardiovascular disease, for example by ‘knowing your numbers’ and getting your blood pressure and cholesterol checked, or having a free NHS health check with your GP in midlife for those living in England.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

Industry observers note that I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

Industry observers note that the “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler claims, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

Industry observers note that there’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting company to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

In a recent development, the best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

Sources indicate that with the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

According to recent reports, and focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:.

Industry observers note that when time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

According to recent reports, pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

In a recent development, include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”.

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Recent findings suggest that sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:.

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

It has been revealed that mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Recent findings suggest that cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

According to recent reports, I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

In a recent development, sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

Breaking: From CUDA and Jax to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Andlukyane

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that some time ago, I shared a blog post about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder.
  • According to recent reports, after optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that some time ago, I shared a blog post about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs. Recently, Google released TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for TPUs, and I wanted to see how well it works on the same task: whether a PyTorch-native TPU stack could match my A100 training pipeline and my JAX beam search in speed and solution quality, or maybe even beat them.

Recent findings suggest that the short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder. My initial training port was 1.65x slower than the A100 implementation, while the first TPU beam search was 5.7x slower than its JAX counterpart.

According to recent reports, after optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially. Training reached comparable wall-clock performance to the A100, and the optimized TorchTPU beam search became 25% faster per level than JAX on the same eight-chip v6e machine, producing the same total solution length across six test puzzles.

Along the way, the investigation improved the solver itself and resulted in an upstream TorchTPU GitHub issue that led to attention-routing fixes.

The code is available on Kaggle notebooks running on a free TPU v5e-8:.

As in the previous post, the code and the experiments were done by coding agents (Claude Code and Codex): I decided what to port, what to measure, and how to judge the results, and they did the implementation and the profiling.

The CayleyPy Professor Tetraminx competition requires finding the shortest sequence of moves that solves 1000 scrambled puzzles. Formally, it is a shortest-path problem in a Cayley graph (each puzzle state is a node, and each of the 24 possible moves is an edge) with an 88-sticker state.

My solver uses beam search guided by a learned neural heuristic — a 3.4M-parameter PieceTransformer. Instead of treating the 88 stickers individually, it groups them into 50 physical pieces, turns each piece into a token, adds a class token (51 tokens in total), and runs four small transformer layers with eight heads of size 32. At the end, an all-neighbours Q head (a head that predicts, for each of the 24 moves, the distance to solved after that move) outputs 24 numbers. So the beam scores all 24 children of a state with one forward pass on the parent.

For training, the signal is a mix of cheap random walks and exact ground truth:.

On the A100, one epoch takes 142.7 seconds. My best checkpoint is epoch 1500 of a 2000-epoch run, about 80 hours in total.

In a recent development, torchTPU is not PyTorch/XLA: there is no LazyTensor tracing, no xm.mark_step(), and no xla_device(). Instead, TorchTPU lowers ATen ops directly to StableHLO and runs through PJRT and libtpu (PyTorch’s core ops are translated straight into XLA’s input format and executed by the TPU runtime). Once you import torch, "tpu" works as a device string just like "cuda".

Three rules matter in practice:.

Sources indicate that I ran the first port on a Cloud TPU machine with four v6e chips, using DDP with one process per chip and a global batch of 512, so each epoch saw exactly the same number of samples as on the A100. Before the code could run on the TPU at all, I had to remove four GPU idioms (masked_select in the loss, boolean-mask indexing when expanding labels, 12 .item() metric reads per step, and sampling training anchors on the CPU instead of keeping the 0.19 GB anchor table in TPU memory). This first working version took 234.8 seconds per epoch, 1.65x slower than the A100. I was able to bring it down to 132 seconds with two changes.

In a recent development, the first win was practically free: turning on fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1). Only the model’s forward and backward pass ran under torch.compile; the rest of the trainer (the random-walk sampler with its 40-iteration loop, label expansion, the loss, and the metrics) ran in eager mode, one op at a time. In default eager mode, that data pipeline took 61.3 ms per step. Wrapping it in torch.compile brought it down to 29.7 ms, while fused eager, which fuses the ops at run time without any code changes, got it to 13.1 ms. The pipeline is many tiny ops, and on this workload they fused better than they compiled; I didn’t profile why, since the cheaper option was also the faster one. Setting that single environment variable dropped the epoch time from 234.8 s to 176.5 s.

According to recent reports, still, 176.5 s was slower than the A100, and the GPU profile didn’t help. On the A100, the input stage and embedding gradient took 67% of the step; on the TPU, the same stage took only 0.96 ms (0.8%), and the model was spending ~90% of its time in attention.

A roofline at the model’s own shapes explained why. A square 8192³ GEMM hits 361 TFLOP/s on one v6e chip, and the model’s QKV and FFN GEMMs hit 212–259 TFLOP/s, while attention ran at 3.0 TFLOP/s. With T = 51 and head_dim = 32, every attention matmul is 51x32x51 on a 128x128 matrix unit (MXU) — roughly 2.5% tile occupancy. Padding head_dim to 128 or T to 64 actually made things slower (0.83x and 0.81x). As a result, attention is about 3% of the model’s FLOPs but about 90% of its time on the TPU.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to keep the same model (for a fair comparison), you need to keep the same shapes and find other improvements. Standard scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) expects (B, H, T, Dh), so the QKV tensor has to be permuted to move the heads to the second dimension. Rewriting attention with torch.einsum keeps the heads in their original dimension and avoids the permutes:.

According to recent reports, the fp32 softmax is there for numerics. On the TPU, the einsum and SDPA versions disagreed by a relative 3.3e-3, so I checked both against a float64 reference on the CPU: both were about 4.6e-3 away from it, because the TPU’s matrix unit uses a single-pass bf16 multiply even for “fp32” matmuls unless you raise torch.tpu.precision. In bf16, keeping only the softmax in fp32 closed the remaining gap between the two versions.

In a recent development, this change was almost rejected. The agent first measured it on the forward pass only, where it looked slower (einsum 5.51 ms vs SDPA 4.56 ms), and discarded it on that basis. Thankfully, I decided to check the full forward+backward pass: the profiler attributed much of the backward-pass overhead to layout conversions around SDPA’s saved tensors, which cost far more than the forward pass saved. Across forward+backward, one layer dropped from 25.14 ms to 14.85 ms (1.69x faster). That pushed the whole epoch down to 132.0 s — 1.08x faster than the A100.

Sources indicate that the most confusing bug was in checkpointing. Saving a checkpoint only from rank 0 is a standard pattern:.

According to recent reports, under fused eager, the tensors in state_dict are still deferred. When rank 0 reads them, it executes a graph that includes this step’s DDP collectives, while the other ranks are already waiting at the next barrier. The checkpoint file would grow to 1.1 MB, then 2.2 MB, and freeze forever while every rank sat busy. The fix is to move the tensors to the CPU on every rank and write the file on one:.

The trap only fires in the mode that gives the speedup, which made it harder to find.

On Kaggle’s free v5e-8 (eight chips, 64 samples per chip), the training notebook run 186 epochs in 7.41 hours, with a median of 142.4 seconds per epoch against the A100’s 144.2 over the same epochs.

Over epochs 177-186, the training loss averaged 15.131 on the v5e-8 and 15.132 on the A100, and top-1 accuracy was 0.488 against 0.483. On exact labels, the TPU checkpoint at epoch 186 is on par with the A100 checkpoint at epoch 200: its best predicted move is truly optimal for 99.0% of states, against 98.9%. The best checkpoint trained eight times longer and is still better.

In a recent development, with training done, the second half was porting my beam search solver (KhoruzhiiSolver, the CUDA beam searcher from the previous post) to TorchTPU. Training needed targeted fixes; the solver needed a rewrite. It relied on torch.unique for deduplication, boolean-mask indexing, and dynamic tensor shapes (cand.index_select(0, unique_pos[:B])), none of which works well on a TPU.

So I wrote beam_tpu.py from scratch in pure PyTorch with fixed shapes across every step. Instead of dropping duplicates, I sort candidates by hash, flag adjacent matches, and assign duplicate scores +inf so topk simply never picks them:.

To share a 1M-wide beam across chips, each chip holds an equal share of the beam slots, and a child’s owner chip is determined by its hash. Every step runs the Q-head forward on local parents, routes children to their owners via all_to_all_single, deduplicates globally on each owner, and runs topk for the next level. States are stored as int8, and the tree bookkeeping stays outside the compiled step so the level counter doesn’t trigger a recompilation.

Recent findings suggest that the search doesn’t go all the way to the solved state: it stops as soon as a beam state appears in the exact depth-6 BFS table (27.8M states), and the table supplies the optimal last six moves. In the first TorchTPU version, this endgame tail (a Zobrist hash and a searchsorted over the table for each level, each ending in .item()) ran as eager ops on the TPU and took ~176 s after a 73 s solve. The JAX driver had always done it in NumPy on the host, so I did the same: identical moves on 3000 checked states, at under a millisecond per state. Running the model over fixed-size chunks inside a single scan didn’t change the step speed, but it kept one copy of the model in the compiled graph instead of one per chunk, shrinking the cached compiled code from 363 to 162 MiB.

I first tested an August pre-release of TorchTPU on six hard scrambles (1M beam, 4x v6e). It matched my JAX kernel on path length (186 vs 185 moves, every path replay-verified) but was 5.7x slower (1973 s vs 345 s). The profile showed that cross-chip all_to_all cost only 0.6 ms per step, while model inference took ~83% of the time. Then I moved to the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 on Kaggle, and the results were surprising: the gap narrowed to 2.8x per beam level, but quality dropped, with TorchTPU finding 194 moves where JAX reproduced its 185.

Because Kaggle has a long TPU queue, I moved to Cloud TPU v6e to debug the 8 moves lost between the pre-release (186) and 0.2.0 (194). Two things had changed in 0.2.0: torch.topk had reverted from a stable tie-breaking order back to an unstable default, and bf16 attention on sequence lengths that are not a multiple of 128 no longer ran the whole module in fp32 (more on attention below).

On eight v6e chips, forcing the old low-index tie-breaking in topk took 0.2.0 from 193 moves back to 187, the pre-release’s number there. But why should tie-breaking change path length at all? On four chips, every fixed tie order I tried (lowest index first, highest first, a random shuffle) gave 185 moves; only 0.2.0’s native order gave 188. Something in the beam was turning tie order into path length, and that something was my deduplication.

Recent findings suggest that because the Q head scores children from the parent, a state reached from two parents arrives as two copies with different scores. My dedup sorted candidates by hash and kept the first copy in each run, and since torch.sort is unstable on both builds, “first” was whichever copy the backend left in front. When 0.2.0 changed the tie order, good states started to disappear because their worse duplicate survived. JAX’s dedup uses a stable argsort on score-sorted buckets, so it keeps the better copy.

Replacing “keep first” with a segment-min over (score, index) (so duplicates always keep their best score) added 0.5% overhead and fixed the matter:.

On ten more puzzles, this fix cut total moves from 319 down to 302, improving seven of them and worsening none.

One regression really was TorchTPU’s: on the same chips, 0.2.0 ran a beam level 1.7x slower than the pre-release. Timing each piece of a level separately highlighted that everything except attention was as fast or faster in 0.2.0. The cause was routing: 0.2.0 sends short attention shapes to its Flash attention kernel, which pads the 51-token sequence to a 128-token tile, so 84% of each score tile is padding. Turning Flash off with torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp(False) puts attention back on the plain XLA path (yes, .cuda. — TorchTPU respects PyTorch’s standard SDPA backend switches, which live under torch.backends.cuda):.

With Flash off, a full beam level is 4x faster than with 0.2.0’s default and 2.4x faster than the pre-release. The 2026-11-04 nightly, which already routes short sequences away from Flash, is as fast as the workaround.

Two things hid this at first. The --fp32-attn arm that I added to test attention precision still went through Flash, so it only made things slower. And PyTorch’s AOTAutograd cache is keyed on the graph, not on the attention backend flag, so a second process quietly reused the Flash-compiled graph and reported identical times until each run got its own cache directory.

Industry observers note that my agent wrote up the measurements and reported the issue to the TorchTPU repository with a Colab reproduction and a table of attention timings across head sizes and sequence lengths. It turned out that the short-sequence fix had already landed on main three days after 0.2.0 was tagged, but it hadn’t been released. The report also noted that a newer routing rule on main would make some 128–256-token shapes slower. The TorchTPU team picked it up, merged a series of attention-routing fixes, and closed the issue on November 21.

Milliseconds per SDPA call on one TPU v6e chip, TorchTPU 0.2.0 · lower is better.

With the dedup fixed and Flash turned off, I reran the comparison on one eight-chip v6e machine with the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 and JAX 0.11.0 (the version in Kaggle’s TPU image).

TorchTPU now runs a beam level 1.25x faster than JAX with the same quality.

On Kaggle’s v5e-8, the picture is closer. TorchTPU with Flash off is still about 10% faster per beam level, but the median scramble takes slightly longer (49.9 vs 48.7 s), because it checks the hit flag only every four levels and runs extra levels, and it found one move more (186 vs 185):.

JAX remains my main beam search solution for now as I have yet to run TorchTPU on a wider beam. And the investigations helped push the JAX kernel further: bounding temporary buffers reduced the compile-time memory for a 128M beam from 39.5 to 12 GiB per chip, and a 256M-state beam works on eight v6e chips.

I started this experiment to see whether TorchTPU could replace my A100 + JAX setup, and on this task it can: the same model trains at the A100’s speed or slightly faster, and the beam search matches JAX on quality and is a bit faster per level.

According to recent reports, however, a native PyTorch API does not eliminate the need for hardware-aware engineering. Static shapes, deferred execution, tensor layouts, compilation caching, and kernel selection all mattered considerably. Optimizations that helped training did not necessarily help inference, and seemingly minor changes in backend behaviour exposed a latent bug in my search algorithm.

The migration also improved both implementations: fixing deduplication reduced solution lengths, the attention investigation contributed to upstream TorchTPU improvements, and revisiting memory management enabled larger beams in JAX.

More broadly, this project demonstrated how AI coding agents can participate in experimental engineering rather than simply code generation. Claude Code and Codex implemented alternative approaches, profiled execution, constructed controlled experiments, investigated regressions, and prepared reproducible bug reports. My role was to formulate hypotheses, choose meaningful metrics, question misleading measurements, and decide which trade-offs were acceptable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in Fresh York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera.
  • TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year.
  • Sources indicate that the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in Fresh York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

Sources indicate that the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Sources indicate that chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in Fresh York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

In a recent development, the exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd newly introduced design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau ….

The iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This T&C Pocket Bici is a folding bicycle made by Tresoldi & Casiraghi, an Italian metalworking firm, in 1963. Unlike the folding bicycles of today that split in half, the components here all fold into the racetrack-shaped frame. The whole thing then fits within its own suitcase. (Brompton bike in the photo for scale.).

Recent findings suggest that the bike's origin story is a bit murky; one auction site claims it was created specifically for the Chinese market, and that 2,500 units were sold. In contrast, BikeFlip says a Chinese group placed an initial order for 2,000 units, but that after T&C produced the first 1,000 units, payment never materialized and the project was scrapped.

I could only find one video of the bike being unfurled:.

Notably that channel is Chinese, so it appears at least some of the production units landed in the originally intended market.

Those wheels are even smaller than the small 16 inch Brompton wheels. Bike Friday managed to package 20 inch wheels into a suitcase. The physics of a larger wheel provide a better ride. I can't even ride 16 inch wheels. These look like scooter wheels.

  • It has been revealed that with iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that iPhone Handoff is a newly introduced feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

According to recent reports, 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

It has been revealed that with iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Sources indicate that simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically upgrade across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

In a recent development, iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

Industry observers note that the biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:.

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no aims to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier noted that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

It has been revealed that have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

Latest Update: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • According to recent reports, data centers already use light in networking.
  • The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

According to recent reports, data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Industry observers note that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The manufacturer’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

According to recent reports, “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” states Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

Industry observers note that VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon claims this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the manufacturer’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Recent findings suggest that the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The firm is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

According to recent reports, both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr notes. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

According to recent reports, free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another major advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

Industry observers note that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” notes Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

It has been revealed that one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Sources indicate that in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

According to recent reports, Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the manufacturer confirmed a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

Sources indicate that the energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main matter is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

Recent findings suggest that “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch states.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” indicates Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the organization’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to rapidly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

LightSolver’s team is right now working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the organization’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi indicates. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

It has been revealed that yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick Fresh, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

In a recent development, the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Upcoming states. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Fresh, Optalysis.

Recent findings suggest that instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

New indicates that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

According to recent reports, how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he claims. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” indicates Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”.

Breaking: Crypto trading still forces users to choose between convenience and control

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A candlestick chart on a dark screen reveals prices sliding lower, mostly in red candles.
  • As security concerns persist across centralized exchanges, a newly introduced generation of trading platforms is attempting to make self-custody easier without recreating the complexity of decentralized finance.
  • Sources indicate that for years, cryptocurrency trading has involved a trade-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A candlestick chart on a dark screen reveals prices sliding lower, mostly in red candles.

As security concerns persist across centralized exchanges, a newly introduced generation of trading platforms is attempting to make self-custody easier without recreating the complexity of decentralized finance.

Sources indicate that for years, cryptocurrency trading has involved a trade-off. Centralized exchanges offer relatively straightforward interfaces, but consumers must generally trust those platforms to hold their assets. Decentralized alternatives allow traders to retain control of their funds, although navigating wallets, blockchain networks, gas fees and bridges can make the experience considerably more complicated.

That divide has become increasingly relevant as security breaches and operational failures continue to expose the risks of centralized custody.

Industry observers note that the challenge for developers is no longer simply to build decentralized trading infrastructure. It is to make that infrastructure accessible enough for people who have become accustomed to the convenience of traditional exchanges.

It has been revealed that london-based cryptocurrency trading platform Byrrgis is among the companies attempting to address that problem. Its public launch on November 24 introduces expanded cross-chain trading functionality, token analysis tools and a simplified wallet experience built around a non-custodial architecture.

Sources indicate that on centralized cryptocurrency exchanges, customers typically transfer assets into wallets controlled by the platform. While this arrangement simplifies trading, it also means customers depend on the exchange’s security practices, financial stability and withdrawal policies.

Non-custodial trading changes that relationship by allowing people to retain control of their private keys and authorize transactions directly from their wallets.

Industry observers note that however, self-custody introduces its own challenges. People become responsible for protecting their wallets, understanding transaction approvals and navigating potential vulnerabilities in smart contracts.

It also does not automatically eliminate exposure to third-party infrastructure, particularly when trading involves cross-chain protocols or external liquidity providers.

The question is whether developers can reduce those operational barriers without introducing fresh forms of dependency.

It has been revealed that “Security and control over funds should not come at the expense of a simple trading experience,” remarked Siraaj Ahmed, CEO of Byrrgis. “With our full public launch, we’re bringing together cross-chain trading, token analysis and portfolio management in one place, while allowing owners to maintain control of their assets instead of handing them over to a centralized exchange.”.

One of the persistent usability problems in decentralized finance is fragmentation.

Industry observers note that trading assets across different networks can require separate wallets, native gas tokens and bridging transactions. Customers may also need to understand which blockchain holds a particular asset before executing a trade.

Byrrgis is attempting to abstract some of that complexity through a trading interface supporting Solana, Ethereum, BNB Chain and, according to the tech giant, Robinhood Chain.

Its cross-chain routing system is designed to let consumers initiate supported swaps with a single transaction signature rather than manually moving assets between networks.

A feature called Universal Gas is intended to remove the need to maintain separate native gas-token balances for supported transactions.

These approaches reflect a broader direction in blockchain development known as chain abstraction, where the underlying network infrastructure becomes less visible to the end user.

Recent findings suggest that yet simplifying the interface does not remove the technical risks of cross-chain execution. Routing systems, liquidity providers and smart contracts can still introduce points of failure, even when people retain custody of their wallets.

Another challenge facing cryptocurrency traders is the amount of information required to evaluate unfamiliar assets.

Market liquidity, trading momentum and on-chain risk indicators are often distributed across multiple analytics platforms, making comparisons difficult for less experienced owners.

Byrrgis has incorporated a feature called Scout Score, which assigns supported tokens a rating between 0 and 100 based on a combination of on-chain risk, market momentum and tradability indicators.

The scores upgrade as market conditions change, offering a consolidated assessment alongside the platform’s token discovery tools.

Such systems may make complex information easier to interpret, but they also raise questions about transparency and reliability.

A numerical score can simplify research, yet its usefulness depends on how indicators are weighted, how frequently data is updated and whether the methodology can identify emerging risks.

A high rating should not be interpreted as a guarantee of safety or future performance.

Beyond cross-chain trading and token analysis, Byrrgis has introduced card-based cryptocurrency purchases, a redesigned wallet onboarding process and changes intended to improve swap execution.

The platform also includes tools for tracking holdings across networks and managing multiple positions from a single interface.

These additions illustrate a wider challenge for decentralized trading applications: competing with the user experience of centralized platforms while preserving the characteristics that distinguish self-custody.
