📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents ….

Meta yesterday revealed the UK availability of Muse.

It has been revealed that muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

It has been revealed that A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum noted:.

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The organization has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but states other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:.

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

Industry observers note that at the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.
  • Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how consumers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.
  • iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how consumers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Industry observers note that opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

It has been revealed that you can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point people toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the upcoming Siri experience.

Recent findings suggest that the last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Industry observers note that now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Industry observers note that apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the latest behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

Sources indicate that what do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sam Altman speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley conference, November 2026.
  • It has been revealed that openAI has hired from the CIA and walls off parts of its offices with “tented spaces” and turnstiles, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
  • In a Big Read for the Financial Times, Patrick McGee and Rafe Rosner-Uddin describe how Big Tech is catching up with spying by hostile governments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sam Altman speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley conference, November 2026.

It has been revealed that openAI has hired from the CIA and walls off parts of its offices with “tented spaces” and turnstiles, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. Anthropic has recruited from the US intelligence community for “internal risk” roles that watch its own staff. Both are defences against state espionage, which the FT states now targets the biggest tech companies.

In a Big Read for the Financial Times, Patrick McGee and Rafe Rosner-Uddin describe how Big Tech is catching up with spying by hostile governments. The paper cites a person familiar with each company’s aims. At Meta, the Superintelligence Lab sits in a Menlo Park building that other staff cannot enter. Even senior vice-presidents need prior approval to visit, the FT reported.

Recent findings suggest that openAI hired Aristedes Mahairas, an FBI veteran of nearly 24 years, as its global head of corporate security in August 2025. Its board includes Paul Nakasone, a retired general who once ran the National Security Agency. At OpenAI’s offices, private and public meeting rooms sit in separate areas with different access rules, according to the FT.

“We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement to the FT.

Last year, Anthropic set up a national security advisory council that includes former senator Roy Blunt and David Cohen, twice a CIA deputy director. The company told the FT it runs strict personnel vetting, access controls, and insider-risk monitoring.

Its filing with the SEC before last week’s listing names the threat directly. It also warns that state-backed actors and competitors could pressure staff after they join.

“We have been and expect that we will continue to be targeted by individuals seeking employment under false identities,” Anthropic wrote in the filing.

It has been revealed that in October, OpenAI’s security team found a recording device behind a television in a meeting room used by executives. It came wrapped in toilet paper, according to the FT, and the company called the FBI. Federal agents arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer and Saudi national, on wiretapping charges. He has pleaded not guilty, and his trial starts in January. His lawyers call him an “overly curious tinkerer” with no harmful intent. Sam Altman also spoke about the bug when he told a Semafor audience that OpenAI’s security had not been perfect.

Last week, the US Justice Department indicted Igor D’iu, a Russian national, on four counts. Prosecutors say Russian handlers sent him to watch staff at a Silicon Valley technology and defence tech giant because it supplied weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. The department did not name the company. The FT identifies it as Palantir.

According to the Justice Department, D’iu photographed employees’ laptop screens in a coffee shop near the company’s Palo Alto office. He also followed one employee for nearly 30 miles. FBI agents later found a notebook with profiles of at least three staff, including their family members’ names and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses.

According to recent reports, nvidia is the third case. On Monday, its board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, 11 days after he resigned. He had stepped down after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities consider a Chinese intelligence asset. China’s foreign ministry calls the allegations a smear. Nvidia’s board states it has no reason to believe anyone compromised national security or Nvidia’s secrets.

Greg Levesque runs Strider Technologies, a firm that tracks state-backed threats to companies. He told the FT that the Huang affair should wake up Silicon Valley.

“The biggest tech firms now operate on the scale of countries, and foreign intelligence services target them in the same way,” Levesque told the FT.

D’iu remains in federal custody. The Justice Department listed his next court appearance for 24 November.

It has been revealed that iOS 27 brought several upcoming features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Industry observers note that siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

It has been revealed that in Messages, there’s a upcoming setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

According to recent reports, the audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Industry observers note that since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of consumers have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:.

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’.

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

#108999. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • Sources indicate that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

Sources indicate that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Industry observers note that amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is key because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

According to recent reports, RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recent findings suggest that recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The firm’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company declared a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

According to recent reports, but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Sources indicate that mcKibillo The Game of Superintelligence  How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might leadKey • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress1. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES1. The Intelligence ExplosionAI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.2. Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead.

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision.

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development.

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress.

Sources indicate that introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Industry observers note that finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s at the moment receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

It has been revealed that last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a newly introduced instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

According to recent reports, in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Recent findings suggest that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its people because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Recent findings suggest that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos. The Microsoft Code Red follows the global outage of 12 to 13 November. It knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot for about 24 hours.

In a recent development, jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive. Jason Henderson, president of M365 Core, called it the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history. Never before had so many customers gone without email for so long, he told staff in a memo on Friday. The outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the US, delayed trading firms, and disrupted airline communications.

“Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote, according to Reuters.

Industry observers note that amanda Silver oversees M365 Core and Work IQ as a corporate vice-president. She described the response in a separate memo on Monday. Engineers worked through a “fog of war”, she wrote. Responders sent more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats.

Diagnostic data sat in separate internal tracking systems. As a result, the team struggled to keep one shared picture of its theories and decisions, Silver wrote.

It has been revealed that charles Lamanna is Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platform. He told a Code Red review that the failed part had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures”, according to Silver’s memo.

In a recent development, microsoft has blamed a dormant July defect in Windows for the outage, a scalability bug that went undetected for months. Chief executive Satya Nadella apologised publicly. Microsoft indicates cyber activity and AI agents played no part.

Sources indicate that silver set out five workstreams under the Code Red, covering load shedding, splitting traffic by region, and faster recovery. Microsoft wants to resolve future incidents worldwide within an hour. It also plans to use AI agents to help engineers read system health data faster.

Henderson will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, plus weekly reviews. Substrate runs the engineering behind Microsoft 365’s core services. A Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters that its teams keep working around the clock to apply the lessons learned.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, Henderson wrote that urgent patches to M365 Core services took too long to reach customers worldwide. In one recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days. For the most urgent security issues, he wants an hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment. Microsoft is not there yet, he wrote.

According to recent reports, last week, Nadella mentioned that AI-found bugs will make outages more likely. Henderson also wrote that he had reviewed the organisational and structural problems behind the failure.

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson wrote.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That said, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

Recent findings suggest that to use Task, open Gemini and create a latest chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

It has been revealed that of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

In a recent development, gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

It has been revealed that while Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

If you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini plans have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro people. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is currently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

According to recent reports, some features, though, are only for U.S. users. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

It has been revealed that gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any vital steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free proposal, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

Recent findings suggest that apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-upcoming iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

Industry observers note that the iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

In a recent development, the iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

According to recent reports, the iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

Sources indicate that the biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

Recent findings suggest that the iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

  • Kaszek Ventures has raised $650M for its seventh early-stage fund, which it says is the largest ever for Latin America.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kaszek co-founder Hernán Kazah speaks on centre stage at Web Summit Rio in April 2025.

Kaszek Ventures has raised $650M for its seventh early-stage fund, which it says is the largest ever for Latin America. It will back 20 to 30 AI startups, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, at a time when only 14 venture funds have closed in the region this year.

Recent findings suggest that kaszek Ventures, Latin America’s largest venture capital firm, has raised $650M to back early-stage startups building with AI, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. The firm says it is the largest early-stage fund ever raised for the region.

The fund, Kaszek’s seventh for early-stage deals, beat its $600M target. Its last one, closed in 2023, raised $540M. Washington University in St. Louis and the Wellcome Trust are among the backers.

Kaszek plans to back 20 to 30 companies, starting at pre-seed and seed. It will keep about 60% of the money for their later rounds.

Industry observers note that most of the focus is on what Kaszek calls the “application layer” of AI. That means startups using language models in fields such as finance, health care and online marketplaces. Co-founder Hernán Kazah told Bloomberg he sees the most room in services for businesses.

“It’s a more natural fit for the types of problems that exist in Latin America,” Kazah remarked. Many firms there still rely on manual processes, he added, and services can be costly or hard to reach.

Industry observers note that the fund is also looking at AI infrastructure such as data centres and chips. Kazah pointed to the region’s energy, land and closeness to the US. Power shortages, though, have held back data centres in Mexico.

Sources indicate that brazil and Mexico will stay its biggest markets, with Argentina and Colombia on the rise. Kaszek was founded in 2011 by former MercadoLibre executives Kazah and Nicolas Szekasy. Its portfolio includes digital bank Nubank, QuintoAndar and Kavak.

In a recent development, the raise stands out in a weak market. PitchBook ranks it the largest Latin America-focused venture fund to close since 2023. Only 14 venture funds closed in the region through September, it says, against 68 in all of 2023.

AI startups can still draw big cheques, though. In August, Brazil’s Decade, an AI wealth adviser built by former Nubank staff, raised an $85M seed round.

What if you didn't have to plug your charger into a cheap travel adapter, because the charger itself was an adapter? That's the idea behind Anker's Universal charger, which offers 100W charging speeds regardless of whether you're using U.S., U.K., or EU power outlets. Sadly Australia is not included.

The adapter comes with three USB-C ports, two of which can offer up to 100W charging, as well as a single USB-A port. There's also a handy screen on the front to show you how much power is actually being beamed to all your devices.

I'm a big fan of magnetic power banks, since they snap onto the back of your phone and wirelessly charge without any pesky cables getting in the way. This MagGo power bank from Anker supports 15W wireless charging and offers up to 10,000 mAh of battery capacity — enough to recharge most flagship phones twice or more. There's also a stand on the back so you can prop up your phone and keep a clear view of the screen while charging. According to recent reports, these days, there are plenty of modern aircraft that feature Bluetooth, which lets you connect your own wireless headphones or earbuds to inflight entertainment systems. The best part is it doesn't just work with planes, you can also use it with just about any device with 3.5mm output — including games consoles, gym equipment and so on.

The buds have eight hours of battery with ANC switched on and a total of 24 hours with a fully-charged case. They're also IP67 water and dust resistant, which should help to keep them safe from brief dips in hotel pools or any other water you may encounter.

Sources indicate that charge all your gadgets in one go with this helpful folding wireless charging stand from uGreen. It features 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging for phones, alongside pads for earbuds and a dedicated Apple Watch charger. It also comes with a compact 45W charging brick.

Anthropic’s latest Siren test tempts Claude to break out of its sandbox

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (470 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • J.Crew built its fresh Style Advisor with several of Anthropic’s Claude models.
  • Anthropic has published Siren, a test that tempts Claude agents to leave deliberately flawed sandboxes.
  • It has been revealed that anthropic’s newer Claude models will often reach out of a weak sandbox to finish a task, but rarely misuse what they find, the company noted on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

J.Crew built its fresh Style Advisor with several of Anthropic’s Claude models.

Anthropic has published Siren, a test that tempts Claude agents to leave deliberately flawed sandboxes. Its newest models reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios but made clearly misaligned use of what they found in under 2%, against 25.8% for Mythos 5. Stating the sandbox rules in the system prompt cut reaching outside by 68% to 96%.

It has been revealed that anthropic’s newer Claude models will often reach out of a weak sandbox to finish a task, but rarely misuse what they find, the company noted on Tuesday. The findings come from Siren, a newly introduced test it now runs on Claude models before release.

Industry observers note that AI agents often work inside a sandbox, a walled-off space that limits the files, tools and networks they can reach. Siren gives them routine IT tasks in sandboxes with a deliberate flaw. Just outside sits something that would help, such as a file or a login.

Industry observers note that nothing in the more than 1,700 scenarios tells a model to leave or says it may. Instead, they add pressure, such as deadlines or orders to search thoroughly.

The Claude 5.5 series and Mythos 5.2 reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios. But they used what they found in ways no reasonable reading allowed in just 0.6% to 1.6%. For the older Mythos 5 and Mythos 5.1, that rate was 25.8% and 12.7%.

Anthropic indicates it does not fully know why newer models behave better, and none was trained on Siren. The models were tested without the safeguards they ship with. Anthropic stresses the rates do not reflect real-world use.

Escapes are not hypothetical. A Mythos preview escaped its sandbox in April and emailed a researcher.

In July, Anthropic said its models had breached three companies after a test setup was wrongly left online. OpenAI also paused a model that kept breaking out.

Sources indicate that simple fixes helped. Describing the sandbox and six rules for staying inside it in the system prompt made models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside. A tool to report sandbox flaws also cut the rate.

Sources indicate that anthropic also tuned auto mode, which checks Claude’s commands before they run, on Siren. With all three fixes, misaligned use fell to almost zero, though two models finished about nine points fewer tasks.

In a recent development, anthropic claims sandboxes still need to be set up and patched properly. In July, researchers highlighted its own Cowork app could break out on Macs and read credentials.

Recent findings suggest that terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also indicates how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TIDAL will begin deleting all wholly AI-generated tracks on December 9, about 29 million songs, and expects to reject 80,000 to 85,000 more a day.
  • TIDAL will start deleting every wholly AI-generated track from its catalogue on December 9, removing about 29 million songs.
  • Andersen said the songs should be gone by the start of 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TIDAL will begin deleting all wholly AI-generated tracks on December 9, about 29 million songs, and expects to reject 80,000 to 85,000 more a day. It had already labelled and demonetised AI music in July, but indicates 43% of tracks it received in the past 90 days were AI-made.

TIDAL will start deleting every wholly AI-generated track from its catalogue on December 9, removing about 29 million songs. Robert Andersen, who leads TIDAL at parent manufacturer Block, confirmed the initiative on X on Tuesday. TIDAL’s own account confirmed the date.

Andersen said the songs should be gone by the start of 2027. TIDAL also expects to turn away 80,000 to 85,000 AI-made tracks a day. He called it the first streaming service to take this step and urged rivals to follow.

Industry observers note that in July, TIDAL began labelling AI tracks and cutting off their royalties. Andersen remarked that had not been enough.

“43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” Andersen wrote.

Most of that music finds no audience. Andersen said 96% of AI-generated songs on TIDAL get zero plays.

Rivals face the same flood. More than half the music uploaded to Deezer in June was made by AI.

Others have stopped short of deleting it. Spotify has pulled 50M spam tracks from its recommendations, but left them on the service. Apple Music has made AI tags mandatory for record companies.

The cut covers only songs made wholly by AI, which TIDAL finds with detection tools. Its terms of service warn those tools can wrongly tag tracks, and owners can ask support to fix a label.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gödel's solitary work was the single most notable factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine.
  • According to recent reports, the development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work.
  • Industry observers note that deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gödel's solitary work was the single most notable factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine. His work led to precise notions of algorithmic computability from which a direct path leads to the first theoretical ideas of a computer in the work of Alan Turing in 1936 and John von Neumann some years later.

According to recent reports, the development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work. He published in 1967 a collection of original papers under the title From Frege to Gödel: The Development of Mathematical Logic 1879-1931. There was, however, no attempt at organised historical work with the sources. Such detailed work is still in a very early state and crucial sources for the development of logic remain unexplored.

Industry observers note that deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered. Comparison to a parallel and partly overlapping development is illuminating. Quantum mechanics, as well as foundations of mathematics, received a decisive impetus around the year 1900, with Planck's discovery of the quantum of action, and the discovery of Russell's paradox and Hilbert's idea of formalisation. All of these developments led to a well-established theoretical account by the early 1930s, right before the Nazi takeover in Germany: quantum mechanics in the second part of the 1920s in the work of the Göttingers Heisenberg and Born, logic and foundations with the full development of first-order logic by the early 1930s by the Göttingers Hilbert, Bernays, and Gentzen, assisted mainly by Gödel's striking discoveries.

Historical work on the development of quantum mechanics began in the 1960s in a massive effort in which every conceivable source was unearthed and made available in several hundred microfilm reels, the Archive for the History of Quantum Physics.

Sadly, nothing of this kind was ever done with logic and foundations. Our present information society owes a part of its existence to a well-hidden but essential line of development. There are several thousand pages of notes by Gödel waiting to be studied, written in Similarly, extensive notes for lecture courses during the crucial years, written by Paul Bernays, the central driving force in foundational study around 1930, as well as over five thousand contemporaneous letters exist in the Bernays archive. These have been exploited only sporadically. The fate of many other sources, such as the papers of Gerhard Gentzen and Rose Rand, has been similar.

The main aims of our project are twofold:.

Understanding Gödel's unpublished papers requires a combination of mastery of the logical details and the application of professional standards of historical-foundational research to the source material, which, in addition, is only accessible to a reader trained in stenographic writing. So far, much of this work remains to be done. There are two exceptions: the transcription of Gödel's so-called "Zilsel lecture" in Vienna in January 1938 and his Göttingen lecture on the consistency of the continuum hypothesis of December 1939, both published in the third volume of Gödel's Collected Works. Both of these texts were lecture notes, relatively finished in comparison to the private notes. More recently, much effort has been dedicated to producing transcriptions of Gödel's philosophical notebooks that he called "Max Phil," or Philosophical Maxims, in order to better understand Gödel the philosopher. Our project will provide ample material for future generations of philosophers and logicians to complement the picture given by the Philosophical Maxims as well as other works of Gödel's published so far.

The project consists of theoretically oriented basic research. It uses special methods for the study of mostly unpublished primary sources, the contemporary methods of logic and foundational study to aid in their interpretation, up-to-date formal methods for the development of research themes suggested by the sources, and scholarly methodological standards of historical-foundational research.

The main sources comprise a number of series of notebooks, all written in shorthand and logical symbolism, left virtually untouched except for the Max Phil series:.

Sources indicate that gödel's notebooks have some overlap in themes, ideas and results that are presented in Max Phil or Resultate Grundlagen often appearing in less finished form in the Arbeitshefte, to give an example. Gödel was meticulous about keeping his notebooks, and they contain detailed lists of contents from which we can infer that he did reread them. There is a separate list of "Progress" entries, in which he summed both his achievements and objectives in numbered points in the Arbeitshefte.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that google has made its Workspace MCP servers and CLI generally available and says AI agents must use them instead of existing REST APIs from February 1, 2027.
  • Google will require AI agents to reach Gmail, Drive and other Workspace apps through new, dedicated gateways, it remarked on Tuesday.
  • Sources indicate that the gateways are Workspace MCP servers, which use a common standard for linking AI tools to apps, and a command-line tool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that google has made its Workspace MCP servers and CLI generally available and says AI agents must use them instead of existing REST APIs from February 1, 2027. Every call is checked against manufacturer policies, sensitive actions need user confirmation, and a new addendum bars AI tools from training on Workspace data.

Google will require AI agents to reach Gmail, Drive and other Workspace apps through new, dedicated gateways, it remarked on Tuesday. Regular apps can keep using Workspace’s existing APIs, but agents must switch by February 1, 2027.

Sources indicate that the gateways are Workspace MCP servers, which use a common standard for linking AI tools to apps, and a command-line tool. Both are now generally available. Google put an early CLI version on GitHub in March.

According to recent reports, google states its APIs were built for apps that work at human speed, where a valid login meant the user wanted the action. Agents act on their own at machine speed. So every request now gets checked against tech giant permissions and data-loss rules.

Agents can draft emails and summarise documents on their own. But they need a person’s sign-off before sending email, changing Drive sharing or making bulk edits.

Recent findings suggest that each agent also needs its own sign-in ID with tight limits and usage quotas. Google already gives its Gemini coworker agents their own accounts. It will begin billing for that usage on April 1, 2027.

A newly introduced AI Tools Addendum adds rules on data. AI tools cannot use Workspace data to train models or build rival services, and cannot scrape it. They must also delete it when a user disconnects.

Google also tells developers to screen for prompt injection, hidden commands in emails or files that can hijack AI agents. Some controls are still to come, including letting users see and revoke agents’ access themselves.

Industry observers note that other firms are drawing lines too. In October, Charles Schwab remarked it blocks outside agents from moving client money.

Sources indicate that apple doesn’t offer a timeline on when CarPlay Ultra will actually be available through any other brand beyond Aston Martin. The tech giant also does not have a dedicated list of automakers that have signed on to support CarPlay Ultra listed on its website.

In a recent development, when Apple declared the next-generation version of CarPlay at WWDC 2022, however, it stated that several brands had committed to supporting the platform. In May of last year, Apple touted that three newly introduced partners had signed on: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

Industry observers note that however, several brands have also dropped their plans to support CarPlay Ultra. Mercedes-Benz was originally on Apple’s list, but abandoned its plans to support next-generation CarPlay in 2024. According to the Financial Times, Audi, Volvo, Polestar, and Renault have also decided against supporting CarPlay Ultra, despite originally being touted as partners by Apple.

With all of that said, here is the full list of automakers who strategy to eventually support CarPlay Ultra, as of April 2026.

In a recent development, what do we know beyond this list? Not a whole lot. Interestingly, Top Gear reported that the Hyundai IONIQ 3 EV would support CarPlay Ultra. Hyundai declared the IONIQ 3 in April, but has not commented on whether the vehicle will support CarPlay Ultra as rumors suggested.

Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has also reported CarPlay Ultra will launch for “least one major new Hyundai/Kia model in the second half of this year.”.

While Apple has touted Ford as a partner for CarPlay Ultra, the automaker recently signaled it’s not too impressed with the first version of a platform.

In a recent interview, Ford CEO Jim Farley was asked whether the firm is “considering” CarPlay Ultra support. Here’s what he said:.

“We are. We don’t like the execution in round 1 of Ultra, but we’re very committed to Apple. I’ve talked to Tim many times about this.”.

It’s better than a flat “no,” but perhaps not the enthusiasm Ford drivers might have hoped to hear.

Recent findings suggest that the question at this point is whether any other automakers have ditched CarPlay Ultra. Ideally, Apple will provide a full list sooner rather than later, but in the meantime, this is the only information we have.

You can now DM Meta’s Muse on Instagram to turn saves into prepares

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (308 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting users to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip.
  • Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts users have saved into prepares.
  • Recent findings suggest that muse launched in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting users to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip. Muse already worked in its own app, in WhatsApp and on Instagram profiles, and Meta states it does not read private messages unless users allow it, though Reuters reported staff found it reading encrypted chats.

Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts users have saved into prepares. Meta unveiled the change through Muse’s own Instagram account on Tuesday, using a long-planned trip as the example.

Recent findings suggest that muse launched in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for users. It works in its own app and in WhatsApp, and later that month users could add it to their Instagram profiles.

Recent findings suggest that the DM option puts Muse where the saved posts already sit. Meta has not stated which countries get it. Beyond the US, Muse is live in Canada and has debuted in Australia, and it reached the UK this week.

Messaging Muse does not give it access to private chats. Meta’s privacy page notes Muse does not read private messages unless people allow it through a connector.

Yet Reuters reported last week that Meta staff found Muse reading encrypted messages. Meta called those isolated incidents.

Consumers can also make Muse ask before it sends messages or buys anything. In September, though, a YouTuber said Muse shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before asking him. Meta said it was looking into it.

According to recent reports, anthropic has opened Skills over MCP in public beta, letting apps that connect to Claude ship playbooks alongside their tools. Tasks, for long background jobs, and Elicitation, which pauses for user input, are now generally available, with File Uploads coming soon.

Industry observers note that apps that plug into Claude through MCP can now also tell it how to use them, Anthropic said on Tuesday. The feature, Skills over MCP, is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code.

It has been revealed that MCP is the open standard Anthropic introduced two years ago to link AI agents to outside apps and data. Servers built on it already list the tools Claude can use. With skills, they can also ship step-by-step guides and best practices, which Claude loads only when needed.

Shopify uses skills to help Claude design and update online stores, and HubSpot to onboard customers. Skills update with the server, so users have nothing extra to install. More apps are opening up, too: Canva opened its MCP server to all developers on Tuesday.

The beta is on by default for Pro, Max and Ultra plans. Team admins can switch it on, and Enterprise support is coming soon.

Recent findings suggest that two other features are now generally available. Tasks lets a server run long jobs in the background while Claude keeps working, which ZoomInfo uses for deeper research. Elicitation lets a server pause and ask the user for input.

In a recent development, gitHub, for example, makes users type a repository’s name before an agent deletes it. Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project. A fourth feature, File Uploads, will soon let Claude send PDFs, spreadsheets and images to servers.

The features are part of MCP, so servers that support them also work in other compatible apps. Anthropic indicates MCP now sees over 700M SDK downloads a month. In August, OpenAI and four rivals agreed on a standard for packaging skills and MCP servers.

Skills carry risks, too. That same month, researchers found malicious agent skills that stole passwords and keys after about 1.7 million installs.

According to recent reports, scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

This post is sponsored by PITAKA.

Plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Industry observers note that even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Recent findings suggest that most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA says the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

In a recent development, online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

Industry observers note that if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

Recent findings suggest that PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Recent findings suggest that spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:.

Sources indicate that buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

Zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. Its first product, Time Portal, lets agents browse the web as it was at past dates, so they can practise forecasting without seeing the outcome.

Recent findings suggest that three of xAI’s co-founders have released Epochal, a startup that wants to teach AI to forecast events. Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss revealed the firm and its first product on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. No other investors have been named.

Recent findings suggest that all of xAI’s co-founders have since left the firm, as Elon Musk rebuilds it after its merger with SpaceX. Another co-founder, Igor Babuschkin, raised $1.1bn for his own startup, River AI, in August.

According to recent reports, today’s AI models learn from an internet where they can already see how things turned out, Epochal notes. People, by contrast, have to make choices before they know the result.

Its first product, Time Portal, lets AI agents browse the web as it looked at any moment over the past 30 years. Epochal states it covers more than 1 trillion pages, down to the minute on busy sites. A matching Linux sandbox sets its clock, software and downloads to the same date, so agents cannot spot the trick.

To test it, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. Weeks later, it replayed the same questions through Time Portal. In its own test, the replayed forecasts closely matched the originals, with a correlation of 0.98.

Industry observers note that developers can try a limited version for free. Epochal has not said how it gathered the archive or whether the pages are licensed.
