Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greynoise

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure.
  • In a recent development, we witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created.
  • The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.

In a recent development, we witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.

Example POST to loginSrp1 and response.

Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested.

2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.

Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.

Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.

The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.

Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant.

They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.

According to recent reports, 2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.

The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.

Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.

Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor rolled out over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.

The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.

2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.

Excerpt from exploit.py -  This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.

2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.

Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.

2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and introduced pull_.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.

Excerpt from pull_.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.

2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.

2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.

Industry observers note that 2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.

2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.

Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.

According to recent reports, all of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.

Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt.

One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.

After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.

2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.

Recent findings suggest that example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened rapidly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) debuted earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

It has been revealed that with AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

Industry observers note that this expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

It has been revealed that with AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company indicates this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

Sources indicate that I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the latest speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that customers are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

#108960. PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1196 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A small transformer that writes and sketches from text.
  • Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive.
  • It has been revealed that so here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson.

Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad.

It has been revealed that so here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt.

Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected.

That’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture.

Almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive.

Sources indicate that the drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them.

Sources indicate that I compared PenGPT with older approaches then changed one thing at a time and retrained. Here are the rows I found most interesting; the paper has the rest.

According to recent reports, data and how you show it. Those are the massive rows. Cut the data and everything gets worse. Drop augmentation and the drawing model stops following its prompts entirely. Train on one word at a time and the model can no longer pick up a hand: style rank goes from 1.9 to 6.0.

The clever parts barely register. Telling the model where its pen is does nothing for handwriting. The BPE merges I was proud of make the score slightly worse; they buy speed (sequences are 3.2x shorter) and that’s all. A vocabulary sixty times larger changes nothing. Doubling the model changes nothing.

Sources indicate that even the transformer is optional, sort of. An LSTM on the same tokens is a bit behind on handwriting and still picks up fresh hands. On drawings, where sequences are several times longer, it falls well behind.

Enough tables. Here’s what the two models make.

According to recent reports, the drawing model takes a few controls besides the prompt. One of them is how much ink to use.

It can also draw some things it was never shown as long as a blend of two familiar ideas will do.

Sources indicate that the trick is almost embarrassingly simple. Each training sequence holds up to four words by one writer. That teaches the model that later words look like earlier ones so at sampling time you hand it a few real words and it keeps going. No style encoder, no fine-tuning. That’s how the 21 hands at the top of this post were written.

It also works from a photo. There are no strokes in a photo so I trace a few of its words with InkSight and fit one new writer vector to the traces, with the rest of the model frozen.

One head in layer 4 puts 81% of its attention on the letter being written. I looked for heads that specialize in cursive or print and found none; every head reads the same positions in both.

Captions are the expensive part of the drawing data. Since SigLIP puts pictures and text in the same space, maybe you could train on picture vectors alone and type a prompt at the end?

Recent findings suggest that you can’t. The picture-only model has the best likelihood of the three and it draws scribbles. The reason is geometric: SigLIP’s vectors for sketches sit in a narrow cone, nearly at right angles to its vectors for text. A model that has only seen the cone is lost when you hand it a sentence. Labels are enough to draw labels (78%) but only captions get you phrases (43% against 10%).

It has been revealed that the drawing model blends but doesn’t bind. A teapot with a face is fine. Who wears the hat is not and “facing left” gives the same drawing as “facing right” because the single vector it’s told is close to a bag of words (those two captions have a cosine similarity of 0.999). Sampled handwriting is also less legible than the real thing, 54% against 66%. And since most of the handwriting was traced from scans, its stroke order is a model’s guess and not a record.

If you look over my blog, you’ll notice that many of my projects revolve around clever ideas. I fell in love with them because they were elegant. That isn’t a flaw in itself but I think Rich Sutton was wise to warn about it in The Bitter Lesson. It really is bitter and it has taken me more time than I’d like to admit to embrace it.

I think this post is my first step in the right direction. The results are interesting and the project was a pleasure to work on. And yet there was no clever architectural idea behind it. About 80% of my effort went into building the biggest, cleanest datasets possible and doing lots of quality control on them. Another 15% went into finding a decent 8xA100 node and getting my models to train fast and in parallel on it: 8 minutes for the handwriting model and about 35 for the sketch model. My previous attempt, the Cursive Transformer, took upwards of 10 hours on an A100 and only ever learned one hand. The tokenizer I used here is much simpler and far less elegant but it just works.

According to recent reports, the bitter lesson kills or sidelines a lot of beautiful research ideas. It’s like gravity: it constrains you and most of the time it’s a very bad idea to fight back. But as I accept it and begin to work with it, I find things to admire. As a physicist I’m fascinated by the emerging science of scaling laws. And as a lover of biology I like the idea of putting a ton of work into the data and then literally growing a model on it, as you would an organism. Then you get to interact with it, learn what it’s capable of and study how it works. Seen this way, the bitter lesson has its own charm.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a tall order for an actor to embody any living person, but especially someone whom audiences may already have negative feelings about.
  • Industry observers note that rather than daunting, that challenge was “exciting” to actor Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI’s polarizing CEO Sam Altman in the film Artificial, slated for an initial Dec.
  • According to recent reports, garfield’s perspective on Altman morphed as he worked to better understand him, the actor told me ahead of an early screening hosted by SFFilm in the heart of the city where the story is set.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a tall order for an actor to embody any living person, but especially someone whom audiences may already have negative feelings about.

Industry observers note that rather than daunting, that challenge was “exciting” to actor Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI’s polarizing CEO Sam Altman in the film Artificial, slated for an initial Dec. 25 release. The biopic follows the rise of OpenAI, focusing on Altman’s relationships — particularly with his cofounder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) — as he relentlessly pursues success amid Silicon Valley’s artificial intelligence power struggle.

According to recent reports, garfield’s perspective on Altman morphed as he worked to better understand him, the actor told me ahead of an early screening hosted by SFFilm in the heart of the city where the story is set. His mission as an actor is to get to the “central truths” of who a person is, he said, “and try to merge my soul with theirs. And like all of us, Sam has so many facets.”.

That includes physical traits. Garfield indicates he had to lose weight and change his gait and voice to try to match Altman’s. The semblance is striking. From his bouncy stride to his clipped, gravelly speech, Garfield effortlessly emulates the Altman we’ve seen in interviews and Congressional testimonies. It’s a remarkable transformation — down to the sly, coaxing glint in his eyes — showcasing the breadth of Garfield’s acting talent.

According to recent reports, but it goes beyond physicality. Garfield had to dig deep internally to find elements “that felt like they were a match” with Altman, he stated. The result is an astonishingly believable portrayal of a multidimensional figure, at once pensive and inscrutable.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a responsibility,” Garfield told me. “I take it very, very seriously to play any character, but particularly someone who’s alive, someone who’s pretty much my age. But also, maybe the greater responsibility is making sure that we interrogate these human beings that are leading our world into the next chapter, it seems.”.

“And it feels like our job as storytellers to reflect the times we’re in,” he added, “and no better way of doing that than by looking at the human beings — their personal relationships, their souls, all the diamond facets of their souls — and interrogate the people that have the power over our culture right now.”.

Artificial explores OpenAI’s rise through a rather bleak lens, with questions of moral responsibility and safety looming over the protagonists as they navigate the firm’s success. The film is laced with dark satire, which offers moments of levity amid otherwise weighty meditations on the technology’s long-term impact.

In one scene, when Sutskever is asked about the difference between AI and artificial general intelligence, which can theoretically match or even surpass human ability, he plainly responds, “It’s like how rocket ships are different from scooters.” He goes on to tell his cohorts that this is achievable “in your lifetime — well, maybe not yours or yours or yours,” as he points to the less youthful figures in the room. Moments like these elicited generous laughter from the audience.

Sources indicate that director Luca Guadagnino, known for deeply character-driven stories, such as Challengers and Call Me by Your Name, remarked he was following the news about Sam Altman’s temporary ousting from OpenAI in 2023 and was fascinated by the “Shakespearean feud” leading to that moment. Guadagnino applies his signature character-centric approach to OpenAI’s story, relying on slow, measured beats, piercing close-ups and suspenseful music to relay the stakes of each pivotal moment.

In a recent development, “It’s never about the object; it’s always about the people,” Guadagnino noted during a panel discussion after the screening. “It’s not about AGI or AI. It’s about the conflict between worldview and way of being, embodied by people that clash or fight for the vision they have.”.

He also said, “The point for me was more about trying to understand: How did the possibility of an incredible technology that can help all of us turn into the opportunity to get power in your hands and to become self-entitled?”.

In a recent development, garfield is no stranger to portraying prominent figures in the tech world, having played Eduardo Saverin, Facebook’s co-founder and former chief financial officer, in 2010’s The Social Network. On the surface, Artificial seems like a spiritual successor, recounting another defining moment in the tech industry. But the films differ in both tone and approach, with Artificial trading rapid-fire drama for a darker, more existential theme that occasionally ventures into more technical territory. What the films do share is a focus on bold, forceful personalities.

“From that experience, I suppose, I was very curious about what it takes to win in this particular late-stage capitalist world that we’re in with these emerging technologies,” Garfield noted during the panel discussion. “What does it take to hold Sauron’s Ring of Power and not be completely burnt up by it? Is it possible to not completely lose yourself to that overwhelming, exponentially growing possibility and power?”.

In a recent development, comic relief also arrives in the form of Ike Barinholtz playing OpenAI cofounder and tech mogul Elon Musk. By portraying him as a brutish, aloof figure who saunters in and out of rooms on a whim, he effectively underscores the absurdity of perceived importance and status. Almost every on-screen moment generated a murmur of laughter in the audience.

“I think we’re all fascinated by these cultural, iconic figures who are leading us into this next stage of culture and society,” Garfield told the crowd. “They’re kind of kids. They’re kind of slightly stuck in an early developmental place, and that felt like a really vital part of Luca’s telling of this story.”.

In fact, he added, “[Guadagnino] would say to us, ‘This is a John Hughes movie. This is a high school, screwball comedy, just with slightly higher stakes — mixed in with a little bit of Invasion of the Body Snatchers.’ A very key part of this is that these are all kind of adolescent, high-school-minded people.”.

Even the way Garfield portrays Altman flippantly perching on couches and sitting cross-legged on tabletops while donning sunglasses — including during serious conversations about the future of OpenAI — was deeply researched.

“We had amazing consultants and researchers that work with us that gave us lots of information that’s not quite in the public arena about our characters,” Garfield mentioned. “And Sam is someone who apparently would always sit like he was crisscross applesauce at play school, nursery school [or] kindergarten.”.

Ultimately, Artificial poses an open question about where society is headed and whether those at the helm are equipped to lead the charge. Amid weighty explorations of AI’s ramifications, the film paints a haunting, revelatory portrait of the cunning, mercurial figures making decisions that shape our world.

For Garfield, this presented an opportunity to dive deep into a figure like Altman, who, despite his prominence, remains largely elusive in the public eye.

In a recent development, “I just wanted to tell this story and actually uncover for myself, excavate for myself, who is this person?” Garfield told me. “I’m dying to understand this person, and I get to try to understand this person, maybe more than anyone else has ever really tried to. And it feels like a gift to me.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that at today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the firm introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks.
  • Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model reveals 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.
  • Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the firm introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model reveals 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

According to recent reports, microsoft notes MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

It has been revealed that this doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

Industry observers note that it’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these latest models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex.

It has been revealed that one thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the manufacturer paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous.

Sources indicate that there’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

Sources indicate that this becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Industry observers note that think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a tech giant is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these fresh models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

It has been revealed that also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first.

A manufacturer with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft claims the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the newly introduced models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open matter.

The manufacturer also described clearly that these newly introduced models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

In a recent development, speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these upcoming models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

Here in the World: Letters of Albert Camus, 1944–1959

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that what an amazing behemoth of a book!
  • On D-Day, Camus was thirty; Casarès was twenty-one.
  • Sources indicate that the correspondence was first published in French in 2017; now it has been (brilliantly) translated by Sandra Smith and Cory Stockwell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what an amazing behemoth of a book! I’ve been lugging it around for weeks. Nearly a thousand letters: the intimate correspondence of Albert Camus and Maria Casarès. When they first met in Paris – on D-Day, 1944 – Camus had already published L’Etranger (1942; The Outsider). Born and raised in Algeria, he was in Paris when the Second World War broke out, and later joined the French Resistance. Camus’s wife, Francine Faure, a mathematician and pianist, remained in Algeria. Maria Casarès was originally from Galicia, the daughter of an exiled former prime minister of Spain, Santiago Casares Quiroga. In 1944, Casarès was already known as an actress, having played the titular role in J M Synge’s Deirdre of the Sorrows. She later starred in Les Enfants du paradis (1945), Cocteau’s Orphée (1950) and La Lectrice (1988), among other films and plays.

On D-Day, Camus was thirty; Casarès was twenty-one. They began an affair, but this ended when Camus was reunited with his wife. In 1945, Faure gave birth to twins: Catherine and Jean. In June 1948, Camus and Casarès met again and embarked on a long relationship, which continued until Camus’s death in a car crash on 4 January 1960. Afterwards, the poet René Char found Casarès’s letters in Camus’s apartment and discreetly returned them to her. In the 1990s, not long before she died, Casarès offered the letters to Camus’s daughter, Catherine.

Sources indicate that the correspondence was first published in French in 2017; now it has been (brilliantly) translated by Sandra Smith and Cory Stockwell. The letters are passionate, voluminous, at times torrential. Everything is discussed: love, sex, books, plays, films, beauty, art, family, madness, fear of failure, fear of death. Also logistics, travel aims, inadequate postal services, money troubles, indigestion, hives, headaches.

In a recent development, in her preface, Catherine Camus writes: ‘Their letters make the earth more vast, space more luminous, the air lighter, simply because they existed.’ Casarès, she believes, is ‘like the ocean: breaking, crashing, re-forming and starting over again with stupefying vitality’. Camus is pretty oceanic as well. Both lovers travelled extensively; the letters are often scrawled in haste, sent from Paris, Cabris, Oran, from North and South America, written on ocean liners, or ended abruptly to catch the post. Sometimes, too, they are written as a sort of diary, across several days. The tempo changes. There are lists, schedules; they want to know what the other has been doing, hour by hour. How many glasses of wine they’ve drunk. What they’ve eaten. Who they’ve seen. There are ecstatic protestations of love. And questions, lots of questions. What happened last night? Are you happy? Did you see a doctor? They both emerge vividly – fascinating, erudite, witty, anxious; flawed and paradoxical.

As Catherine Camus indicates, there is great luminosity; many descriptions of humid summer nights, bright oceans, shimmering mountains. Also, a rich sense of being finite and alive, briefly here in the world: ‘I didn’t sleep any better last night, and tonight it’s so hot, there are so many crickets and stars that I have no hope of falling asleep. At least I can write to you…’ (Camus). Or, ‘Today the sky, which was a drab deep gray this morning, gradually brightened up, and around 2:00, you could just about see the sun peeking through a soft veil’ (Casarès). They struggle with grief, sorrow and anxiety, with physical asperities. Camus endures savage bouts of TB, ‘getting undressed again, letting myself be poked and prodded’. For a while, Francine Faure is depressed, consigned to a hospital, repeating the name ‘Maria Casarès’. Camus and Casarès agonise about her. Sometimes, they argue furiously: ‘You’re stupid, my poor darling!’ writes Casarès, ‘and we must wait for it to pass!’ The war has ended, cities lie in ruins, everything feels untethered and surreal: ‘Of course, the world is still sick, even if I’m well,’ writes Camus. ‘Will we always have to love each other during the Apocalypse, in anguish, in torment?’.

Industry observers note that often, they discuss books and authors. They’re not fans of Hemingway. On reading To Have and Have Not (1937), Casarès writes: ‘I certainly found some well-written pages but, my God, how dusty, dull, gloomy it all is, and it smells so much of rooms with peeling wall­paper, all of them a mess, with the odor of sheets, night sweats and dirty clothes!’ Camus’s response is yet more scathing: ‘Hemingway? It serves you right! Why read phonies with no talent?’ Proust gets a mixed review: Casarès is ‘hooked’, loves the way he writes about nature, but finds the ‘political gossip’ boring. In January 1950, Camus sends ‘bad news’:.

Industry observers note that george Orwell died. You don’t know him. A very talented English writer, who had the same experience as me, more or less (even though he’s ten years older), and exactly the same ideas. He’d been fighting tuberculosis for years. He was one of a very small number of men with whom I shared something.

According to recent reports, both Camus and Orwell opposed the adamantine absolutes of communism and fascism; both were attacked for their political views. They had arranged to see each other in Paris in 1945, but Camus was afflicted by another bout of TB and the meeting never happened. A few months after Orwell’s death, Camus gives a copy of Nineteen Eighty-Four to Casarès. She isn’t convinced: ‘I didn’t learn anything from it that I hadn’t already imagined, and it left a weak impression on me.’.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to his own books, Camus is full of self-doubt, grappling with his ‘tormented, mistrustful soul’. He works ‘like a madman’ on L’Homme revolté (1951; The Rebel), but fears it is a failure: ‘I only hope that this book won’t be too far from what it was meant to be. I hope it will help people to live – that it will say that all is not lost – that it will give everyone with whom I feel solidarity the strength to hate nothing, and to create.’ Even after receiving the Nobel Prize in 1957, Camus is still ‘trying to find some equilibrium within myself’. As for Casarès, in one of the last letters she describes herself as ‘here, a little shapeless, it’s true – a little like you, perhaps, or like the world that surrounds us – but I’m here nonetheless, whole and alive’. It’s impossible to know if they wrote with any sense of eventual publication in mind, or simply and entirely for each other. Camus usually drafted and redrafted his published works. Even his Notebooks were edited – by Camus himself, and by Francine Faure, among others. In the end, these letters are so surreally intimate, so poetic and unbridled, that it feels a bit like reading an extraordinary epistolary novel: about love, art, war, finitude and crazy-­beautiful optimism. All is not lost indeed.

#108954. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (771 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we all know AI can get expensive.
  • Also: Microsoft states its latest AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
  • Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft states its latest AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions.

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:.

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

In a recent development, then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new.

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”.

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving manufacturer labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the manufacturer saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your firm needs a chief AI officer in 2026.

According to recent reports, I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

It has been revealed that microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the organization’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the tech giant’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:.

This means the organization doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella revealed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft says its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several upcoming Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

In a recent development, “As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft remarked. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also declared Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft said, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s upcoming Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft stated the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft noted.

The firm added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also declared a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. At the moment in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up rapidly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

Microsoft also declared that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft confirmed a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the firm’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft demonstrated how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

Recent findings suggest that “It starts with a fresh way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft noted. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

Industry observers note that “Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft stated. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise prepares.

  • Sources indicate that enhancement 11/24: This latest setting is now widely rolling out.
  • Recent findings suggest that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the fresh “Chat content including text & attachments” setting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out latest privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.

Sources indicate that enhancement 11/24: This latest setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Recent findings suggest that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the fresh “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”.

Google is now separating that preference into two upcoming options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:.

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”.

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, consumers, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”.

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “latest settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying consumers via email.

Nvidia announced on Monday that ousted cofounder Jensen Huang would return to his role as CEO after he resigned earlier this month when multiple extramarital affairs became public, including one with a woman that the US intelligence community believes is a Chinese intelligence asset.

“The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” stated Harvey C. Jones, chair of Nvidia’s board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the manufacturer.”.

The stunning news comes after weeks of reporting on alleged malfeasance in Huang’s personal and professional lives. The scandal broke when The Latest York Times reported that Huang had a close, personal relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Then came news of a second extramarital affair, leading to Huang’s eventual resignation.

In a recent development, previously, the board denied it would bring Huang back, despite Huang saying he would return if the board allowed it. Many names were floated as a possible replacement for Huang, including Arm CEO Rene Haas. But many tech experts said it was difficult to imagine Nvidia without Huang. Apparently, the board agreed.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress temporarily took over as interim CEO, telling investors at its recent earnings call that everything is “business as usual.” But additional reporting revealed that Huang regularly “humiliated” his direct reports, raising serious questions about his management style and the corporate culture of Nvidia, which Huang helped shape more than any other person over the past 20 years.

In a recent development, nvidia’s stock price rose dramatically on Monday morning with the news of Huang’s return, dragging with it other chipmakers like AMD and Qualcomm and market indices including the S&P 500, Nasdaq and Dow, which all jumped up on Monday. It’s another sign that Nvidia, as a key manufacturer in the AI industry, is a driving force behind the US and global economy.

The board added that it received input from “senior levels of the United States government” on the decision. President Donald Trump noted in a Truth Social post that Nvidia made the “correct and proper decision” to reinstate Huang, adding, “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the US Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”.

Industry observers note that the board’s independently commissioned investigation into Huang will continue, but he will regain his seat on the board. Huang is still set to testify before the Senate’s banking committee on Dec. 3, and the SEC’s investigation into Nvidia is also still set to continue.

Calling into CNBC’s Squawk Box on Monday morning, Trump reiterated that Huang’s return is good news for the country. He called Huang a “genius,” saying, “We have to protect our geniuses … The bigger threat is losing the brainpower of a person like Jensen.” In a rambling interview, Trump talked about the importance of Nvidia’s industry-leading chips.

Trump previously floated the idea of former Apple CEO Tim Cook taking over Nvidia’s top job, which gained zero traction. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been pushing for further scrutiny of Huang and Nvidia’s compliance with US export control rules. While Trump loosened the rules around how US chipmakers can do business with Chinese companies, there are still bans on selling the most advanced chips.

In a recent development, but we need only look to the stock market to see why the Trump administration may be changing its tune. Since the beginning of the scandal, Nvidia’s stock price has fallen dramatically, wiping out billions in market value. Monday morning’s news of Huang’s return saw premarket trading hike its share price by 30%. With Nvidia, so goes the entire stock market. And after last week’s Anthropic IPO failed to quell concerns over a growing “AI bubble” — where Nvidia is smack-dab in the center — the rebound points to investors’ confidence in Huang, Nvidia and the AI industry, spies and affairs be damned.

Within Silicon Valley, some have continually pushed for Huang’s return. Elon Musk posted an ominous “It is done” on Monday morning; Epic CEO Tim Sweeney posted a link to AC/DC’s Back in Black, a nod to Huang’s affinity for expensive black leather jackets.

It has been revealed that the tech industry, perhaps more than any other, thrives on the narrative of the god-like startup founder. It’s why Jensen Huang was synonymous with Nvidia, Sam Altman with OpenAI and Dario Amodei with Anthropic. And this is not the first time a major tech CEO’s departure has caused such a commotion.

“[Huang’s] return may help restore investor confidence, but the upheaval echoes Sam Altman’s brief ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI,” Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne stated, “raising similar questions about corporate governance and the outsized influence of individual leaders over the future of AI.”.

According to recent reports, altman was fired and reinstated within a chaotic five-day period in 2023. The OpenAI board accused Altman of lying to them, but he was ultimately welcomed back and has kept a firm grip on the now-huge AI organization ever since. This episode is the basis for Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming movie, Artificial, starring Andrew Garfield as Altman, coming out next month.

Those tech founders have become increasingly intertwined with government power, particularly since Trump’s return to office. Many Substantial Tech executives, including Huang, have donated billions in personal funds for Trump’s projects, such as his inauguration fund and aims for a White House ballroom. It’s led many tech critics to argue that Big Tech is buying influence to avoid regulation and oversight.

In a recent development, “​For years, Major Tech has used ‘national security’ as a pretext for killing pro-competition, kids’ privacy, and AI safety bills,” remarked Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of the Tech Oversight Project. “But when their favorite CEO’s indiscretion helps a foreign rival, those concerns are thrown out the window in favor of protecting their own interests.”.

Industry observers note that during the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella unveiled several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the manufacturer. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its fresh AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.

According to recent reports, MAI mentioned it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

Recent findings suggest that the approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft remarked it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman stated during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

It has been revealed that the dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the manufacturer has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Industry observers note that western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026.

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman mentioned of the upcoming coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The organization also released its fresh image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

#108942. Charging to 100% Every Night Wears Down Your Phone’s Battery. Try This Instead

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1075 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Charging to 100% Every Night Wears Down Your Phone’s Battery. Try This Instead

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple claims iPhone batteries are most comfortable at temperatures between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit, and charging outside that range, whether in a hot car or inside a thick case, speeds up wear.
  • Recent findings suggest that voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss.
  • It has been revealed that age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple claims iPhone batteries are most comfortable at temperatures between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit, and charging outside that range, whether in a hot car or inside a thick case, speeds up wear. Heat is one of two things that age a phone battery faster than normal use. The other is time spent at 100%. Avoiding both takes very little effort, and the charge limit settings on iPhones, Pixels and Galaxy phones handle part of the job for you. Here’s how to charge in a way that keeps your battery healthier for longer.

Recent findings suggest that voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss. The damage may not appear immediately, but it’s measurable after one year and obvious after two.

It has been revealed that age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably. Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity faster when they spend extended time at the top of their charge range, which is precisely where an overnight charge leaves them. The fix doesn’t require a fresh phone or even a new charger. It requires a small adjustment to a habit most people have never thought twice about.

According to recent reports, keeping a lithium-ion cell pinned at 100% creates voltage stress, and the heat generated from sitting on a charger could end up meaning the difference between keeping your current phone a little longer or having to buy a upcoming one. So once and for all, does keeping your phone plugged in really hurt the battery? Here’s what the experts suggest.

Recent findings suggest that it isn’t about immediate damage but rather how fast your battery ages over time. Understanding the difference between what will and won’t break your phone is key. Here is the truth about your charging habits.

Battery health is not just about how many times you charge your phone. It is also about how it manages voltage, temperature and maintenance. Lithium-ion batteries age fastest when they are exposed to extreme levels: 0% and 100%.

Sources indicate that keeping these batteries near full charge for long stretches of time puts additional voltage stress on the cathode and electrolyte. This is why many devices use “trickle charging” or temporarily pause at 100%, topping up only when needed.

Still, the biggest threat is not overcharging, but heat. When your phone is plugged in and running demanding apps, it produces heat that accelerates chemical wear inside the battery. If you are gaming, streaming or charging on a hot day, that extra warmth does far more harm than leaving the cable plugged in overnight.

The Apple battery guide describes lithium-ion batteries as “consumable components” that naturally lose capacity over time. To slow that decline, iPhones use Optimized Battery Charging, which learns your daily routine and pauses charging at about 80% until just before you typically unplug, reducing time spent at high voltage.

Recent findings suggest that apple also advises keeping devices between 0 and 35 degrees Celsius (32 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit) and removing certain cases while charging to improve heat dissipation. You can read more on the official Apple battery support page.

Sources indicate that samsung offers a similar feature called Battery Protect, found in the One UI battery and device care settings. When enabled, it caps charging at 85%, which helps reduce stress during long charging sessions.

Recent findings suggest that other Android makers like Google, OnePlus and Xiaomi include comparable options — often called Adaptive Charging, Optimized Charging or Battery Care — that dynamically slow power delivery or limit charge based on your habits. These systems make it safe to leave your phone plugged in for extended periods without fear of overcharging.

Even with these safeguards, some conditions can accelerate battery wear. As mentioned before, the most common culprit is high temperatures. Even for a short period of time, leaving your phone charging in direct sunlight, in a car or under a pillow can push temperatures into unsafe zones.

It has been revealed that heavy use, such as gaming or 4K video editing, while charging can also cause temperature spikes which can degrade the battery faster. And cheap, uncertified cables or adapters may deliver unstable current that stresses cells. If your battery is already several years old, it will naturally be more sensitive to this kind of strain.

In a recent development, there is no need to overhaul your habits, but a few tweaks can help your battery age gracefully. Start by turning on the optimization tools on your phone: Optimized Battery Charging on iPhones, Battery Protect on Samsung devices and Adaptive Charging on Google Pixels. These systems learn your routine and adjust charging speed so your phone is not sitting at 100% all night.

According to recent reports, keep your phone cool while charging. According to Apple, phone batteries perform best between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit (16 to 22 degrees Celsius). If your phone feels hot, remove its case or move it to a better ventilated or shaded spot. Avoid tossing your phone under a pillow or too close to other electronics, like your laptop. Skip wireless chargers that trap heat overnight. Use quality chargers and cables from your phone manufacturer or trusted brands. Those cheap “fast-charge” kits you find online often deliver inconsistent current, which can cause long-term challenges.

Finally, try not to obsess over topping off the charge. It is perfectly fine to plug in your phone during the day for short bursts. Lithium-ion batteries actually prefer frequent, shallow charges rather than deep full cycles. There is no need to keep it between 20% and 80% all the time, but just avoid extremes when possible.

According to recent reports, keeping your phone plugged in overnight or on your desk all day will not destroy its battery. That is a leftover myth from a different era of tech. Modern phones are smart enough to protect themselves, and features such as Optimized Battery Charging or Battery Protect do most of the heavy lifting for you.

Still, no battery lasts forever. The best way to slow the inevitable is to manage heat, use quality chargers and let the software on your phone do its job. Think of it less as “babying” your battery and more as charging with intention. A few mindful habits today can keep your phone running strong for years to come.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet.

According to recent reports, I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is right now expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

Also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why.

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

According to recent reports, desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful.

One thing that surprised me is that Myna (Ubuntu’s AI dictation tool) has yet to find its way into the Ubuntu ISO as a default app. As with Ubuntu 26.10, you can install it, but you have to first add the necessary repository with:.

With the repository added, you can install it with:.

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

Recent findings suggest that it’s so early in the release cycle that it still uses the default 26.10 wallpaper, but there will be more information soon. I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

Also: Linux has hundreds of distros: 5 reasons to stop using the same few.

It’s been a very long time since Canonical had a disappointing release, and 27.04 will keep up that trend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving update. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch users can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Also: Pixel Watch 4 vs. Watch 5: Is Google’s newly introduced model worth it?

In a recent development, constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

In a recent development, wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how promptly it can drain.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 review: Health data overload, but built for the future.

The upgrade improves battery life without customers having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

That’s not the only Google Play Services update that Wear OS smartwatch customers can take advantage of. Another recent update lets users view on their phone a larger preview of any watch face they want to install on their smartwatch.
